Introduction: Acute kidney injury (AKI) appears to be prevalent in ICU COVID-19 patients. Nevertheless, there are few data in comparison with non-COVID-19 patients. The aim of our study was to compare the prevalence of AKI in COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 critically ill patients.

Methods: We performed a retrospective single-center study including all consecutively COVID-19 critically ill mechanically ventilated patients admitted from 03/2020 to 11/2021 to our ICU and all consecutively critically ill mechanically ventilated patients from 08/2020 to 01/2021 and from 03/2021 to 08/2021 admitted to our non-COVID-19 ICU. Patients' demographics, comorbidity including Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), outcome, as well as, admission, maximum and minimum creatinine blood values, as well as KDIGO stage were recorded. Two patient groups, i.e., COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 patients were compared in terms of AKI.

Results: The study included 333 patients (183 COVID-19, 150 nonCOVID-19), of an average age 66.3 ± 14.36 years-old. Between the two patient groups there was no difference in age or sex. COVID-19 patients had a lower CCI score (84% had a score of < 5 compared to 68.8%, p = 0.004). COVID-19 patients had a lower admission creatinine (1.13 ± 0.78 mg/dl vs 1.49 ± 1.33 mg/dl, p 0.003), nevertheless, developed more often AKI (74.3% vs 54%, p 0001) during their ICU hospitalization. Among COVID-19 ICU patients that developed AKI 54.4% were stage 1, 18.8% stage 2 and 26.8% stage 3, while 10.27% (19/185) of patients underwent CRRT. Twenty-eight-day mortality was high in COVID-19 patients (66.18%, 90/136). There was no difference in KDIGO stage percentage among the two groups.

Conclusions: COVID-19 critically-ill patients develop more often AKI compared to non-COVID-19 patients. More studies are required to assess this phenomenon, focusing also on the long-term follow-up of the kidney function of these patients.

Introduction: Urinary chemokine C-C ligand 14 (CCL-14), an immunological mediator, is a promising biomarker of renal functional non recovery after acute kidney injury (AKI) [1, 2]. We aimed to evaluate the impact of its use in clinical practice.

Methods: A single-center, prospective, observational study of critically ill patients with stage 2 or 3 AKI by KDIGO criteria on ICU admission was performed. CCL-14 was measured on fresh urine within 48 h of admission and 48 h afterwards using the NEPHROCLEAR TM CCL14 Test (Astute Medical ® ). Patients with stage 5D chronic kidney disease; expected length of stay in ICU < 48 h; renal replacement therapy (RRT) in the week prior to ICU admission; and patients with a clinical decision to start RRT prior to study inclusion, were excluded. A questionnaire was made to the clinician in charge of the patient before and after each CCL-14 measurement.

Results: Thirty-nine patients were included, of which 58% men, 90% caucasian. 66.3 year-old, median APACHE II 24 and SAPS II 54. 23% developed persistent AKI and 7 required RRT. Patients with persistent AKI, had a first CCL14 median value of 7.49 and second of 4.5. Those who required RRT, had a median CCL14 value of 7.34 ng/ml. Patients with transitory AKI, had a first CCL14 median value of 1.2 and second of 1.05. When asked, 2.6% and 7.7% of clinicians answered RRT should be started; 23.1% and 30.8% believed RRT would be needed in the next 48/72 h; 71.8% and 66.6% thought drugs dose should be adjusted, before and after knowing the CCL14 value respectively. 20% changed their fluidtherapy goal after knowing CCL14 value.
Conclusions: CCL-14 may be useful for clinical practice decisions and future studies are needed to evaluate its use on hard outcomes.

Introduction: Knowing the potential for persistent AKI (vs recovery of renal function) is crucial, as these patients are at increased risk for adverse outcomes, including 90-day mortality, renal replacement therapy, and persistent renal dysfunction. We aimed to evaluate urinary chemokine C-C ligand 14 (CCL14) as a valid biomarker to predict persistent severe acute kidney injury.

Methods: A single-center, prospective, observational study of critically ill patients with stage 2 or 3 AKI by KDIGO criteria on ICU admission was performed. CCL-14 was measured on fresh urine within 48 h of admission and 48 h afterwards using the NEPHROCLEAR TM CCL14 Test (Astute Medical ® ). Patients with stage 5D CKD; expected length of stay in ICU < 48 h; renal replacement therapy (RRT) in the week prior to ICU admission; and patients with a clinical decision to start RRT prior to study inclusion, were excluded.

Results: Thirty-nine patients were included. Of these, 18 patients had an initial CCL14 value of less than 1.3 ng/ml, 19 with a value ≥ 1.3 to < 13 ng/ml, and two patients with dosages greater than 13 ng/ml. In 67% of cases there was no change in the value range in both assessments. 23% (n = 9) developed persistent acute kidney injury, the vast majority with stage 3 AKI on admission. CCL14 was significantly higher in end point positive at enrollement (7.34 ng/ml vs 1.22 ng/ml). CCL14 dosing higher than 1.3 ng/mL was associated with an increased risk of developing persistent AKI, odds ratio (OR) 2 (95% CI 0.4-9.5). High CCL14 values are also associated with the need for RRT in the first 5 days. 7 patients required RRT, with a median CCL14 value of 7.34 ng/ ml; OR 2.6 (95% CI 0.4-15.8).
Conclusions: Elevated CCL14 values correlate with the development of persistent severe acute kidney injury. These data may lead to a paradigm shift in the approach of these patients.

Introduction: In recent years, lactate levels have been associated with neurological outcomes in patients undergoing extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR). We hypothesize that donor lactate level could also be a good predictor for immediate graft function after uncontrolled kidney donation after refractory cardiocirculatory death (uDCCD) Maastricht class II.

Methods: A retrospective, non-interventional, ethical committee approved study was designed in a university tertiary hospital, ECMO referral Centre. Data was collected from electronic files of donors and recipients. Regarding the donors, warm ischemia time and lactate levels were gathered. Regarding the recipients, immediate graft function and creatinine at 1 month follow-up were analyzed. For statistical analysis we used SPSS ® software.

Results: From 2017 until May 2022, twenty-one effective donors were identified in our ECPR/uDCCD program. Thirty-one grafts were transplanted. Mean age of donors was 46.7 years and 16 were male. Time from cardiac arrest to hospital admission was 15 ± 8 min, mean lactate level at admission was 21.4 ± 0.5 mmol/l. Regarding immediate graft outcomes, 29% (n = 9) had immediate graft function, 61.3% (n = 19) had delayed graft function (defined as need for dialysis in the first week after transplant) and 9.7% (n = 3) had primary nonfunction. Conclusions: In our study, lactate level of potential donors at hospital admission was correlated with the risk for primary graft nonfunction after kidney transplantation after uDCCD. Introduction: This study aims to determine the incidence of acute kidney injury (AKI) in patients undergoing emergency laparotomy, and whether this correlated with subsequent progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Perioperative AKI is an important contributor to morbidity and prolonged hospital stay [1]. In addition, individuals with AKI are nine times more likely to develop CKD, a progressive and lifethreatening disease [2]. Despite this, there is limited literature of the incidence of perioperative AKI & correlation with progression to CKD.

Methods: A retrospective observational cohort study was conducted using patients identified from the National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) database over a 2-year period within a single London hospital setting. 253 patients were identified. Creatinine and eGFR were collected from premorbid baseline, admission and day one postoperatively and used to determine perioperative AKI. Creatinine and eGFR were collected at 6 weeks and 3 months to determine progression to CKD. KDIGO (Kidney Disease Improving Global Outcomes) criteria for AKI and CKD were used [3].

Results: 16.6% of patients had an AKI on admission with 5.8% of those having a persistent AKI postoperatively. 11.5% of the patients without an AKI on admission developed an AKI immediately postoperatively. 0 patients from either cohort had an AKI at 1 week postoperatively or developed CKD. 2.3% of patients had CKD on admission, but this did not progress over the time period studied.

Conclusions: In this small, single centre pilot study, there was not a single case of perioperative AKI progressing to CKD. More research is required on a multicentre level to further describe the incidence of perioperative AKI and subsequent progression to CKD.

Methods: All adult patients with AKI stage 1-3 and sepsis (Sepsis-3 criteria) on their first ICU stay were extracted from the MIMIC-IV database (Boston, MA, USA [2]). Introduction: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a frequent and severe complication of COVID-19 infection in ICU patients. Introduction: Our goal is to describe outcomes of critically ill COVID19 patients submitted to renal replacement therapy (RRT), in particular the association of RRT with mortality. Methods: This is a retrospective observational study of 338 critically ill patients admitted with COVID-19 pneumonia in the ICU of a tertiary center in Portugal, between March 2020 and December 2021. Introduction: The aim of this experimental study was to elucidate if different distances between central venous catheter tips can affect drug clearance, during continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT). Central venous catheters (CVC) are often used in intensive care patients for drug infusion. If a patient receives CRRT, a second central dialysis catheter (CDC) is required. Where to insert CVCs is directed by guidelines but there are no recommendation how to place multiple catheters [1]. If a drug is infused in a CVC with the tip close to the CDC, it could be aspirated into the dialysis machine and by that, increasing the risk of elevated drug clearance [2]. This phenomenon of direct aspiration has been described in vitro , in case studies and in one experimental study [2-4]. If there is a difference in clearance, when CVC and CDC tips are at different positions is less described.

Methods: In this experimental model with 18 pigs, gentamicin (GM) and vancomycin (VM) were infused through a CVC, during CRRT. Clearance was measured when the tip of the CVC was 2 cm caudally of the tip of the CDC, at the same level and at 2 and 4 cm cranially of the tip of the CDC. Position was controlled by chest radiography. Serum and dialysate concentrations were sampled after 20 min of CRRT at each position. Clearance was calculated. Repeated measure ANOVA was performed, level of significance was set to p < 0.05.

Results: When GM and VM were infused through a CVC the distances between the CVC and CDC tips affected clearance of GM (F = 2,91, p = 0.05) and VM (F = 2.98, p = 0.04), during CRRT (see Fig. 1). Clearance was higher when infusion was in a CVC tip cranially to the CDC tip.
Conclusions: The distance between CVC and CDC tips can affect drug clearance, during CRRT.

Introduction: Strangulating bowel obstruction should be treated immediately. Contrast enhanced CT is widely accepted to classify bowel obstructions. However, the diagnostic imaging criteria are not clearly defined. Accuracy of diagnostic imaging varies with physicians and even specialist can overlook strangulating bowel obstructions. We use AI models to standardize diagnostic imaging and improve clinical outcome of these disease. In this study, we aimed to develop and validate deep neural network (DNN) models detecting strangulating bowel obstruction using contrast enhanced CT.

Methods: We retrospectively collected 31,100 anonymous contrast enhanced CT images together with their clinical reports at the Kishiwada Tokusyukai Hospital between January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2022. We excluded incomplete, younger than 7 years old, and poorly depicted images. The part of this dataset from August 1, 2022, until December 31, 2022, was used for external test and the rest for training and validation. We develop and evaluate two binary-classification DNN models: slice model examining a CT slice to find lesions; series model examining a series of CT images to find a suspected patient. Accuracy, and Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curves (AUCs) were used to assess the models.

Results: The training and validation dataset contained 25,860 images. The test dataset contained 5240 images. The series model achieved 80% accuracy and an AUC of 0.72 for detecting strangulating bowel obstruction, the slice model achieved 72% accuracy and AUC of 0.62.

Conclusions: Our results show that DNN models can potentially identify strangulating bowel obstruction using contrast enhanced CT. Increasing the number of samples, DNN model could accurately detect strangulating bowel obstruction.

Methods: We conducted an open-label phase I safety and feasibility investigation of kefir given in escalating doses to adult critically ill patients with intact gastrointestinal tracts, starting with 60 ml, then 120 ml 12 h later, followed by 240 ml daily. Gastrointestinal symptoms were monitored daily while patients received kefir in the medical intensive care unit.

Results: 52 patients participated (mean age 64 years (range 23-88), 62% male). No serious adverse events were observed other than diarrhea in two patients who also had documented laxative use. The median Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation II score was 35.5 (IQR 23.5-56.9). Kefir was administered via gastric tube to 28 patients, and the rest took it orally. Of the 370 doses ordered, 336 were administered (91%) and met our feasibility target (NPO status was the most common reason a dose was not given). There was no evidence of bacteremia related to kefir. Two patients discontinued study participation due to distaste and bloating.
Conclusions: Administration of kefir to critically ill adults appears to be safe and feasible. A larger evaluation of its safety, tolerability, and impact on dysbiosis and outcomes is warranted.

Introduction: Murine studies indicate that the gut microbiome may influence immunity. However, it is largely unknown whether this also applies to systemic immune responses, especially in humans. If so, profiling the gut microbiota may aid precision medicine approaches in critically ill patients.

Immunological phenotypes were determined using (1) an ex vivo challenge model in which monocytes were stimulated with various inflammatory compounds, and (2) an in vivo challenge model of systemic inflammation and immunological tolerance induced by repeated intravenous administration of 1 ng/kg body weight E. coli endotoxin. Results: Redundancy analysis (RDA) revealed that the gut microbiota composition was associated with sex, but not with age, BMI, or diet (Fig. 1a). A number of pairwise correlations between Blautia, Bacteroides and Prevotella genera and cytokine production induced by these stimuli were identified (Fig. 1c). Conclusions: Although the gut microbiota composition does explain some of the variance in ex vivo cytokine responses, its predictive value is limited. Furthermore, the gut microbiota composition is neither associated with in vivo systemic immune responses to endotoxin in humans, nor with immunological tolerance. Introduction: Loss of muscle mass may be a predictor of mortality in major burn patients, since patients who develop skeletal muscle tissue degradation have longer hospital stays, prolonged mechanical ventilation. Methods: Prospective longitudinal study performed using ultrasound of the quadriceps muscle of the thigh to assess the change in thickness in millimeters on day 1, day 3, and day 7 after study enrollment, in 45 burn patients admitted to a burn treatment center (BTC) of a University Hospital, between April 2020 and September 2021. Patients with burns on the thighs, which prevented the performance of the exams, were excluded.

Results: Correlation was observed between the variation in muscle thickness in the interval from Day 1 to Day 3 and age ( p = 0.035). Loss of muscle thickness was observed in all patients between Day 1 and Day 7. The median thickness for all patients on Day 1 was 24.50 mm (ITQ 21.22-30.85) and on Day 7 it was 18.80 (ITQ 16.07-23.62), with p = 0.0001. The median quadriceps muscle thickness of the patients admitted to the ward on Day 1 was 27.35 mm (ITQ 21.00-35.00) and on Day 7 it was 22.35 mm (ITQ 15.70-27.90), with p = 0.038. The median thickness of patients admitted to the ICU on Day 1 was 23.40 mm (ITQ 21.30-27.00) and on Day 7 it was 18.00 mm (ITQ 16.67-22.02), with p = 0.0005.

Conclusions: Muscle loss occurred early and rapidly within the first seven days of hospitalization. An association was observed between loss of muscle thickness and age, but no association was observed with the extent of the burn, hospital stay, occurrence of healthcareassociated infection, or mortality.

Introduction: First proposed by Dr. Rosenberg, sarcopenia, the loss of skeletal muscle mass, involves a decline in clinical performance, increased mortality and morbidity. In the critically ill patients in ICU, mortality is still a challenge, particularly for elderly patients with functional decline. The relationship between mortality in ICU critically ill patients and sarcopenia is inconsistent throughout literature, impeding our ability to quantify the magnitude of the problem. Our primary objective is to evaluate the role of sarcopenia in the mortality of the critically ill patients in ICU through a systematic review.

Methods: This systematic review was conducted using the Cochrane, Embase and PubMed databases to examine the studies available for the association between sarcopenia and mortality in the critically ill patients.

Results: Overall, eleven retrospective cohort studies totalling 2029 patients, all aged 65 years of age and older, were included in our review with the primary outcome of all studies being mortality. As far as the methods of skeletal muscle measurement using Computerized Tomography (CT) are concerned, six studies used skeletal muscle index (SMI) (n = 832), three studies used skeletal muscle area (SMA) (n = 711) and two studies used total psoas muscle area (TPA) (n = 486). The use of SMI demonstrated an increased risk of mortality in critically ill patients with sarcopenia with 95% confidence interval (CI) = 1.752.82. Similar results were also shown using SMA (CI = 2.73-4.47) or TPA (CI = 1.85-6.30).

Conclusions: Evidently, these results illustrate that critically ill patients in ICU with sarcopenia hold a greater risk of mortality compared with patients without the condition. Effective intervention programmes such as early mobilization and high protein diet can help reduce the mortality risk and provide beneficial outcomes.

Introduction: Although early enteral nutrition (EN) may prevent muscle catabolism, it is concerning in sepsis because of increased risks of intestinal ischemia. We aimed to redefine the evidence regarding the effectiveness and timing of early EN using a systematic review that focused on critically ill patients with sepsis.

Methods: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Cumulative Index to Nursing and Allied Health Literature, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP databases on February 23, 2022. Our systematic review included studies published after 2004 that compared outcomes of early EN with those of delayed EN in critically ill patients with sepsis aged ≥ 18 years. Two authors independently reviewed the title, abstract, and full text and selected relevant studies according to the inclusion criteria. Two authors independently extracted patient information and reports on effectiveness, adverse effects, and clinical outcomes.

Results: Ten studies were included, and the sample size was 31-2410. The pooled risk ratio of mortality obtained using three randomized controlled trials was 1.02 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.85-1.24; ­ I 2 = 3.15%, p = 0.26), which was not significant. The pooled mean difference of length of stay in the intensive care unit obtained using two randomized controlled trials was -1.52 days (95% CI -3.18 to 0.15; ­ I 2 = 47.62%, p = 0.17), which was not significant. The pooled risk ratio of intestinal ischemia obtained using two randomized controlled trials was 3.53 (95% CI 1.36-9.15; ­ I 2 = 0.00%, p = 0.53); this was significantly predominant for early EN. Other outcome measurement indices and adverse effect reports had mixed results.

Conclusions: Early EN intervention did not significantly improve intensive care unit-related mortality but increased intestinal ischemia risks in critically ill patients with sepsis. Heterogeneous characteristics and outcome measurements should be improved for a tailored approach to early EN in critically ill patients with sepsis.

Introduction: Safe extubation is only possible if the patient is conscious and cooperative, able to cough, swallow and has preserved protective reflexes of the respiratory and swallowing tract. Despite that, according to the current recommendation, after extubation they do not receive any liquid orally for 2 h and therefore they feel thirsty. However, there is a lack of evidence in the literature about the validity of this recommendation. The aim of study was to investigate the incidence of thirst and occurrence of complications between patients receiving sipping immediately after extubation and patients who did not drink any fluid within 2 h after extubation.

Methods: In randomized study we assigned 40 patients after short intubation and who were extubated within 48 h. We defined 2 groups with 20 patients in every group. 1st group-early initiation of oral fluid intake in a form of sipping within 2 h, with maximal amount of water 100 ml per hour. 2nd group-oral fluid intake postponed up to 2 h after extubation. Exclusion criteria: patients after upper digestive tract surgery, trachea surgery and with possible neurological deficiency. At defined time points (0, 60 and 120 min after extubation) we evaluated thirst and occurrence of complications (nausea, vomiting, aspiration) between both groups.

Results: Despite the fact we did not find a significant difference in the feeling of thirst at time pointsp > 0.05 (probably because of low number of patients, but tendency is obvious), we found, that in the 1st group where patients received sipping, we saw a significant thirst relief in every time point-0, 60, 120 min after extubationp = 0.0009, 0.0088 and 0.0003. There were no differences in occurrence of complications between both groups.

Conclusions: The study shows that early initiation of fluid intake after extubation, in a form of sipping, seems to be beneficial and safe for patients and decreases incidence of thirst after extubation without any complications.

Introduction: Critically ill COVID-19-patients are at high risk of developing ICU-related malnutrition. Results: 32 patients were included (prone n = 16). Both groups were comparable in age, sex, comorbidities, biochemical markers and Nutrition Risk Screening on admission. Time on IMV was longer in the prone group ( p = 0.032). The total time in prone position ranged from 19.5 h to 13.16 d. All patients received a NG tube, 1 proned patient received a jejunal tube. 6 received TPN ( p = 0.654). Metoclopramide was used more often in the prone group ( p = 0.028). The prevalence of vomiting (n = 4 vs. n = 5), large gastric residuals (n = 0 vs. n = 3) and VAP (n = 11 vs. n = 10) were comparable for the non-prone vs. prone group, resp. However, when correcting for SAPS III-score, the impact of proning declined.

Conclusions: These limited data suggest there is no significant difference in feeding COVID-19 patients on IMV that need proning vs. those who do not, except for metoclopramide use. Introduction: A large percentage of critical illness survivors suffer due to loss of muscle mass, polyneuropathy and myopathy which occur during the early phase of ICU admission and are correlated with increased ICU and hospital stays. In order to manage this physical sequela of critical illness, a specific approach has been adopted: physical rehabilitation. In the ICU, rehabilitation is used to reverse muscle catabolism, reduce the effects of immobility and improve physical functioning. Our main outcome is to investigate the effect of physical rehabilitation in ICU specifically on the outcomes of patients, the dose-response profile and the impact it has on task-specific training.

Methods: We conducted a systematic review using the Ovid Medline, Cochrane and Embase databases to explore the current studies available on physical rehabilitation in the ICU. We included all randomized controlled trials which investigated physical rehabilitation in the ICU in adults. Physical function, muscle strength, hospital and ICU stays, health-related quality of life and mortality comprised our outcomes.

Results: We included sixty-five trials, with a total of 5658 participants. Results showed that physical rehabilitation decreased hospital length stay by 1.77 days (mean difference, 1.77 d: 95% CI 3.05-0.48 d), ICU length of stay by 0.7 days (mean difference, 0.70 d: 95% CI 1.39 TO 0.25 d) and physical function at the hospital discharge has been improved (mean difference, 0.24; 95% CI0.00-0.46). In trials which investigated functional exercises and low-dose physical rehabilitation, the intervention was more effectual compared to the control. Lastly, there was no impact on the other outcomes caused by physical rehabilitation.
Conclusions: We concluded that physical rehabilitation in the ICU overall decreased the hospital and ICU length of stay and improved physical function.

Introduction: Long-term prognosis, especially for post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) is an emerging problem in critically ill patients. Prevalence and risk factors are unclear in patients with severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). We aimed to investigate the prevalence and risks of mortality and PICS in ventilated patients with COVID-19.

Methods: A multicenter prospective study was conducted on ventilated patients with COVID-19 infection. The questionnaire for PICS evaluation was mailed within a median of 6 mo after hospital discharge, concerning Barthel Index, Short-Memory Questionnaire, and Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale scores.

Results: 251 patients completed the PICS questionnaires with a prevalence of PICS of 58.6%, along with the highest percentages of cognitive impairment. Delirium (OR 2.34, p = 0.03) and the duration of mechanical ventilation (OR 1.29, p = 0.02) were identified as independent risks for PICS. In 297 patients who received mechanicalventilation for 7 day or longer, protein and energy delivery in day 4-7, especially for protein delivery, were independently and monotonically associated with in-hospital mortality, but not with PICS occurence.

Conclusions: 60% of the ventilated patients with COVID-19 suffered from PICS. Delirium and longer mechanical ventilation were identified as risks for PICS. In the patents requiring longer mechanical ventilation, nutrition delivery in the late period of the acute phase might be imprtant to survive COVID-19.

Cork University Hospital, Anaesthesiology & Intensive Care Medicine, Cork, Ireland

Introduction: The purpose of this study was to evaluate the functional status and ongoing respiratory symptoms of patients who have been discharged home, who were admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) with severe COVID-19 disease. Long term complications post critical illness, such as post intensive care syndrome (PICS), are well-recognised [1], however, little data exists specific to COVID-19 ICU survivors.

Methods: Local ethics committee approval was secured. Participants were recruited using the electronic intensive care chart database. All patients, from March 2020 to November 2021, who survived Covid-19 were included. Researchers conducted phone interviews with participants and completed three questionnaires; Katz Index of Independent Living Questionnaire, Karnofsky Performance Status Scale and the American Thoracic Society (ATS) Respiratory Disease Questionnaire. Data was input and analysed using excel and stored on a password encrypted computer.

Results: Database search revealed 61 patients available, 33 of 61 patients were included. 20 (61%) were male, 13 (39%) were female. Mean age was 58, with a range of 25-81. Mean length of ICU stay was 15 days, with a range of 1-74 days. 15 (45%) patients were intubated. Most common Katz score (range 1-6) was the highest score of 6 in 23 (70%) patients. Most common Karnofsky score (range 10-100) was 60 in 11 (33%) patients, with 31 (94%) scoring < 100. The most frequent ATS shortness of breath (SOB) grade (range 0-4) was 3 in 10 (9%) patients, with 23 (70%) patients scoring > 0. 14 (42%) patients had an ongoing cough, 11 (33%) patients had a wheeze and 0 (0%) patients were on home oxygen therapy.

Conclusions: This study highlights in the majority of patients who survived severe Covid-19 disease to discharge home, there were serious ongoing limitations to their functional status and exercise tolerance, however, they remained independent of basic activities of daily living.

Introduction: Working on an ICU ward is considered a physical as well as mentally challenging profession which has already been objectified by multiple studies in the past. When the Covid-19 pandemic started, medical staff were suddenly exposed to even greater levels of stress not only at work but also due to social restrictions. Our primary aim of this cross-sectional study is to observe the evolution in time of the impact on mental health during as well as after the pandemic.

Methods: In this cross-sectional study the mental health of our ICU nursing staff (n = 18) was monitored over a period of 26 months by using validate questionnaires for anxiety, depression, insomnia and post-traumatic stress syndrome (PTSD) such as the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) score, Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ9), Insomnia severity index (ISI) and the revised version of the Impact of Event Severity scale (IES-r). In total it entailed 4 surveys during the pandemic and one follow up survey 6 months after.

Results: Regarding GAD7 and ISI, ICU nurses did not score significantly at the beginning nor the end of this study. IES scores started off at 18 which is just below significant but 35% had a score associated with developing PTSD. These scores remained relatively high throughout the pandemic but saw a mean downward trend at the end ( p = 0.338). Mean PHQ-9 scores were initially at the level of 'minimal depression' and rose to be classified as 'mild depression' at the end of the pandemic. In the follow-up survey scores dropped back to 'minimal depression' . In time, the PHQ-9 test was not withheld as significant ( p = 0.298).

Conclusions: It is evident that the results presented in our study show that ICU nurses are prone to developing mental health problems during times of increased workload and stress and in particular the development of PTSD remained high in some subjects. Although there was a slight decrease in our follow-up survey, we believe mental health should be closely followed upon in the future.

Introduction: Manipulations with continuous syringe infusions in the ICU are time-consuming and cost-intensive. Nurses often have to exchange syringes at preplanned times, but pre-emptive swapping of syringes may result in considerable unused residual volume, and thus additional waste. During vasopressor infusion, automated infusion relay is usually considered for ensuring a smooth switching between syringe pumps. However, infusion relay also allows the optimal use of drug solutions and could present an opportunity to reduce environmental footprint and lower costs. Consequently, we studied the magnitude of unused drug disposal in our ICU in a context of manual syringe exchange, to evaluate the potential benefit of an automated infusion relay function.

Methods: We performed a prospective study over 3 weeks in a 32-bed tertiary university adult ICU. All patients, except strictly isolated patients (e.g. with COVID-19, MRSA or ESBL) were included. All 50 ml syringes that were disposed of before or after use were separately collected per patient and the constituent solution and the remaining volume were recorded. Medication costs, as used internally in our hospital, were identified for the 20 most commonly used drugs or solutions.

Results: A total of 2667 syringes from 105 subsequent adult ICU patients were collected and analyzed (Fig. 1). Expired medication or discontinuation of medication accounted for disposal of 179 (7%) completely filled syringes. The 2488 remaining syringes had a mean ± SD residual volume of 12 ± 13 ml (24%). This remaining medication volume had an associated cost of € 5736 or 28% of total cost of fully filled syringes, or at least € 100,000 on an annual basis.

Conclusions: In our ICU approximately a quarter of syringe solutions are discarded during syringe switching. In terms of waste production, associated nursing time and associated material costs, more efficient syringe exchanges with automated infusion relay may address these three concerns.

St Thomas Hospital, Pharmacy, London, UK
Critical Care 2023 , 27(S1) : P340

Introduction: Medication errors are common in critically ill patients with a reported average of 1.7 medical errors each day [1]. Critically ill patients are at increased risk of medication error and patient harm, due to complex medication regimens with frequent changes, organ dysfunction increasing potential for harm from medication errors, and greater use of intravenous medications are associated with increased errors. Many hospitals have policies mandating an independent second check for high risk medication administration such as intravenous drugs or Controlled Drugs, with the intention of improving safety by identifying and preventing errors reaching the patient. This second checking process has a significant time implications and the efficacy for error prevention is debated with adherence to second checking being documented between 52 and 72% within literature [2, 3]. The aim of this study was to determine the barriers for a robust independent second check of medication within adult critical care.

Methods: Four focus groups were conducted with critical care nurses at Guy's and St Thomas' Foundation Trust. Thematic analysis was undertaken to identify potential barriers to implementing an effective second check. Themes were then analysed for thematic content by three critical care pharmacists and grouped with evidence to support or refute the themes.
Results: Subthemes and themes are described in Table 1. The main themes identified as barriers to an independent second checking were complex processes, IT, routine, personnel and geography.

Conclusions: Our study identified a number of common themes associated with failures to implement an effective second check for medication in a critical care. The main barriers identified were personnel, geography and routine. Overall, ethnographic studies are required at ward level as a bigger piece of research to try to further understand second checking.

Implementation of clinical pharmacy services in the ICU
FD Duchi
AZ Groeninge Kortrijk, Hospital Pharmacy, Kortrijk, Belgium Critical Care 2023 , 27(S1) : P341

Introduction: Because of the severity of the disease, the use of highrisk medication, the high frequency of changes in medication charts, and polymedication, patients admitted to the ICU are at high risk for the occurrence of clinically relevant drug-related problems (DRPs). One way to reduce the risk of DRPs is the presence of a hospital pharmacist in the ICU. Since Belgian healthcare is organized differently and the presence of a hospital pharmacist in ICU teams is not well established, a study was conducted to implement clinical pharmacy services.

Methods: A prospective non-controlled interventional six-week study was conducted in a 31-bed intensive care unit in az groeninge Kortrijk, Belgium. The hospital pharmacist was involved in the evaluation of the medication chart of the patient, attending medical rounds, and answering drug-related questions. Clinical interventions were presented to physicians. The acceptance rate was measured, and potential risk factors associated with the acceptance rate were identified.

Results: A total of 204 DRPs were detected. Physicians accepted 158 interventions, resulting in an acceptance rate of 77.5%. Statistical analysis showed that the acceptance rate was significantly associated with the type of proposed intervention. The intervention to change a drug and to pause or stop a drug was implemented more frequently.

Conclusions: Providing patient care to critically ill patients by a multidisciplinary team is an emphasis of the modern day ICU because the team approach is invaluable. Through proactive participation in evaluating the appropriateness of the medication chart, identifying and reporting DRPs, and proposing evidence-based interventions, the pharmacist contributed to the multidisciplinary team in the ICU. Quality improvement by the implementation of clinical pharmacy resulted in high acceptance rates of proposed interventions and high appreciation for the presence of a hospital pharmacist from health care providers in the ICU.

Introduction: Adverse drug reactions (ADRs) remain a huge burden on health care, leading to significant morbidity, mortality, and costs. Based on different literature resources, the prevalence of ADR-related hospital admissions ranges from 0.2 to 54.5% [1]. The costs of an ADR have been reported to be substantial with an additional $6000-$9000 for each event [2]. The aim of this study was to determine the frequency, probability, and severity of ADRs and ADR-related costs in patients admitted to the ICU.

Methods: This prospective consecutive study was carried out in the ICU of Kaunas Hospital of the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences from September 2021 to November 2022. Adult patients admitted to the ICU because of an ADR were included. The probability of suspected ADRs was evaluated using the Naranjo Scale. The severity of ADRs was assessed by the Modified Hartwig and Siegel Scale.

Results: A total of 768 patients were admitted to the ICU during a 15-month period. Of them, 43 (5.6%) admissions were related to ADRs. The mean age of patients admitted due to ADRs was 76.7 years (SD 13.8; range, 33-97). Most of the suspected ADRs (74.5%) were classified as probable; 16.3%, as definite; and 9.3%, as possible. The majority (93%) of ADRs were categorized as severe (of them, 32.5% resulting in death) and the remaining ADRs were moderate. The most commonly reported ADR was bleeding (53.5%) followed by hyponatremia and bradycardia (each 14%), diarrhea (11.6%) and other such as coma, pulmonary edema, etc. (7%). The costs per event ranged from € 502 to € 11,280. Health care expenditures attributed to ADR-related admissions to the ICU totaled more than € 172,000.

Conclusions: Our study showed that the overwhelming majority of ADRs were severe and one-third of them led to a fatal outcome. This warrants future studies on preventability and solutions how to reduce the costs of ADR-related ICU admissions.

Improving drug preparation during emergencies and rapid sequence induction in the adult intensive care unit
I Canisius, A Brown, C Lambert
St Mary's Hospital, Adult Intensive Care, London, UK

Introduction: We aimed to improve efficiency and safety in preparing emergency and rapid sequence induction drugs (ERDs). Critically ill patients are exposed to multiple drugs, and the fast-paced ICU environment is an accepted contributor towards error [1]. Emergencies and intubation involve particularly high-risk injectables, and errors may have devastating effects. Drug preparation may be delegated to doctors of varying experience, causing potential error or delay. We instituted dedicated ERD preparation stations containing drugs, equipment and a quick-Reference table. As per European guidance [2], we introduced pre-filled syringes of drugs that would otherwise need dilution, to avoid miscalculation and extra steps.

Methods: Efficiency and safety in ERD preparation was assessed pre- and post-intervention. Doctors were surveyed regarding knowledge and confidence levels. Two subsets of 10 doctors completed a practical task pre- and post- intervention to record the time taken to prepare a full set of ERDs. They were each given a drug Reference table to mitigate prior knowledge as an influencing variable. Participants completed feedback to identify equipment and process factors that they felt caused delays or risk of error.

Results: 20 pre- and 11 post-intervention survey responses were collected. 91% of responders felt that the new stations had improved safety and efficiency. There was a 61% increase ( p = 0.003) in awareness of drug locations post-intervention. In the practical assessments, the average time taken to prepare a full set of drugs decreased from 20 to 7 min pre- to post-intervention ( p = 0.00009).

Conclusions: Dedicated drug preparation stations have improved efficiency and drug location knowledge. The stations will be extended to other trust ICUs, where we aim to re-audit with a larger sample. Quantifying impact on drug error rate and associated avoidable patient harm requires longer-term study.

Introduction: The impact of frailty on critically ill cancer patients remains to be elucidated. We sought to assess its prevalence in this cohort and its impact on acute outcomes and 90-day post hospital discharge health related quality of life (HRQoL).

Methods: Single centre, prospective, cohort study conducted in the intensive care unit (ICU) of a tertiary care, cancer hospital. All consecutive adult patients with cancer, admitted to ICU over a 10 months period were included in the study. Patients on end-of-life care were excluded. Frailty was assessed upon ICU admission using the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS version 2.0) by two independent investigators [1]. Data pertaining to demographics and outcomes were documented. The acute outcomes analysed were requirement for respiratory and vasopressor support, time to mobilization, ICU readmission, ICU length of stay (LOS), hospital LOS and in-hospital mortality. Patients were followed-up at 90 days post hospital discharge with a phone interview to assess their HRQoL using the EuroQol 5D 5L questionnaire [2].

Results: A total of 516 patients were included in the study. All of them were diagnosed to have frailty (77.9% mild). There was moderate interobserver agreement on CFS (0.552 kappa coefficient). Advanced age ( p = 0.046) and malnutrition ( p = 0.027) were found to be significant risk factors. All acute outcomes, namely, requirement for respiratory ( p < 0.01) and vasopressor ( p < 0.01) support, time to mobilization ( p = 0.01), ICU readmission ( p < 0.01), ICU LOS ( p < 0.01), hospital LOS ( p < 0.01) and in-hospital mortality ( p = 0.01) were adversely affected by frailty. Patients with higher frailty reported significantly poorer health scores ( p = 0.01) and had worse performance among four out of the five dimensions in EQ 5D 5L at 90 days.
Conclusions: Critically ill cancer patients have a high prevalence of frailty and this adversely affects acute outcomes and 90-day post discharge HRQoL.

Introduction: Frailty is associated with a risk of worse outcomes and higher health services use in adult patients undergoing cardiac surgery. In this study we assessed the impact of baseline frailty status on health-related quality of life (HRQL) at 12 months following cardiac surgery.

Methods: This prospective cohort study included patients aged 50 years and older who underwent non-emergent surgery between November 2011 and March 2014 in two adult cardiac surgery programs in Alberta, Canada. Frailty was defined as a Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) score of 5 or greater. HRQL was assessed using the EuroQol 5-domain 3-level (EQ-5D) and Short Form-12 (SF-12) surveys in person pre-operatively and by telephone at 6 months and at 12 months after surgery. Patient socio-demographics, comorbidities, surgery details, cardiac surgery risk scores, adverse events and discharge disposition were also collected.

Results: The cohort (529 patients) mean (SD) age was 67 (9) years. 25.9% were female and the pre-operative prevalence of frailty was 9.6%. Patients with frailty were older (median [IQR] age 75 [65-80] v. 67 [60-73], p < 0.001) and had higher EuroSCORE II (8 [6-9] v. 5 [3-7], p < 0.001). SF-12 physical component score increased from baseline to 12-months in frail (27.5 [9.4]-38.2 [11.9], p < 0.001) and non-frail patients (37.0 [11.4]-47.3 [9.9], p < 0.001). Mental component score in patients with frailty was similar (47.7 [12.0]-52.2 [10.4], p = 0.29) and increased in non-frail (51.8 [10.7]-54.9 [8.5], p < 0.001). Mean (SD) EQ-5D VAS increased in frail (46.2 [18.9]-60.3 [21.6], p < 0.001) and non-frail (60.2 [20.2]-76.6 [15.4], p < 0.001).

Conclusions: HRQL was more impaired in patients with frailty at baseline although incremental improvement in HRQL was reported in frail and non-frail patients over 12-months post-operatively. Recognizing the risk to HRQL among patients with frailty pre-operatively requires further exploration to identify potential interventions to optimize outcomes.

Introduction: Frailty is a valuable predictor for outcome in elderly intensive care unit (ICU) patients. Physicians in ICU often describe patients as 'frail' in Reference to their pre-morbid condition and possibly their chances of recovery following ICU admission. Several validated scores to assess frailty have been developed, such as the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and the Modified Frailty Index (MFI). These scores correlate well with post-operative and post-ICU mortality [1-3]. Nonetheless, in our clinical experience, ICU physicians more often opt to use their clinical judgement, or 'eyeball assessment' , to estimate the degree of frailty.

Methods: A retrospective study of patients admitted to a single center ICU in a large academic medical center in Tel Aviv during March and April 2019. Physician-perceived frailty, as reported on admission on an ordinal scale of no frailty, mild, moderate, or severe frailty, was compared with results of validated scores such as CFS and MFI calculated retrospectively from patient records.

Results: 100 consecutive patients were included; 60 [60%] were male, mean age 58 ± 18 years. The Spearman Correlation test measured a correlation of 0.31 ( p = 0.002) between physician-perceived frailty and CFS and 0.1 ( p = 0.326) between physician-perceived frailty and MFI. On multivariate logistic regression, physician-perceived frailty was found to be independently associated with 30-day mortality (OR 2.16, p < 0.001; Fig. 1) but not with the duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU or hospital stay.

Conclusions: In this single-center, retrospective study, no correlation was found between physician-perceived frailty and CFS or MFI scores. Nevertheless, physician-perceived level of frailty was significantly associated with 30-day mortality. Larger and prospective studies are needed to ascertain these results.

Introduction: To investigate and compare the clinical features and prognosis of chronic critical illness (CCI)/persistent inflammation immunosuppression and catabolism (PICS).

Methods: This is a prospective observational clinical study. During this study period, we collect ICU patients' data from Suzhou Municipal Hospital and Suzhou Ninth People's Hospital. All patients older than 18 years of age were included and according to the corresponding exclusion and diagnostic criteria, they were divided into four groups: PICS group, CCI group, CCI and PICS group (CCI + PICS), nor CCI and nor PICS group (NCCI + NPICS), collected and recorded age, sex, hospital time, hospital diagnosis, acute physiological and chronic health status score II (APACHE II), sequential organ failure detection score(SOFA), c-reactive protein(CRP), absolute value lymphocyte count (L),serum albumin (Alb), white cells count (WBC), absolute value neutrophils count (N), secondary infection and 28-days case fatality rate separately.

Results: A total of 687 patients were admitted to the ICU during the study period. The hospitalization time less than 14 days were excluded and 168 patients were eventually included. There are 17 in the PICS group,71 in the CCI group,50 in the CCI + PICS group and 30 in the NCCI + NPICS group. Baseline characteristics showed statistically significant differences in SOFA, length of hospital stay, 28-day mortality among four groups. Baseline, main indicators and multiple comparisons showed that the CCI + PICS group had longer hospital stay,worse prognosis and more adverse outcomes. Multivariate analysis showed that final age, CRP on day 14 and 21, serum albumin on day 1 and 21 had an impact on the prognosis ( p < 0.05).

Conclusions: The clinical prognosis of the four groups decreased in order of NCCI + NPICS, CCI, PICS, CCI + PICS. Our finding of clinically isolated PICS may indicate that PICS acts as a trigger or independent factor to worsen the prognosis of CCI.

Introduction: Intensive care unit (ICU) survivors are at higher risk of developing mental illness. We aimed to examine the prevalence and associated factors of newly developed mental illness among ICU survivors of critical illness. Moreover, we examined the association between newly developed mental illness and the 2-years all-cause mortality.

Methods: All adult patients ( ≥ 20 years) who were admitted to the ICU during hospitalization between 2010 and 2018 and survived for 1-year were defined as ICU survivors and were included in this nationwide population-based cohort study. ICU survivors with a history of mental illness before ICU admission were excluded from the study. Depression, anxiety disorder, bipolar disorder, insomnia disorder, and substance abuse were considered as mental illnesses.

Results: A total of 1,316,776 ICU survivors were included in the analysis, and 21,274 survivors (1.6%) had newly developed mental illness within 1-year of ICU admission. Old age, longer ICU stay, increased Charlson comorbidity index, hospital admission through the emergency room, increased total cost of hospitalization, mechanical ventilator support, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation support, and continuous renal replacement therapy were associated with an increased prevalence of newly developed mental illness. Moreover, the newly developed mental illness group showed a 1.71-fold higher 2-years all-cause mortality rate than the no mental illness group (hazard ratio: 1.71; 95% confidence interval: 1.65-1.77; p < 0.001).

Conclusions: In South Korea, 1.6% of ICU survivors had newly developed mental illness within 1-year of ICU admission. Moreover, newly developed mental illness was associated with an increased 2-year all-cause mortality.

Introduction: The aim of this study was to compare prevalence of readmissions and death between sepsis and non-sepsis hospitalizations the first year after discharge, and to investigate what diagnoses sepsispatients present with at readmission. Introduction: While clinical role transition is known to pose a challenge to doctors in training, and the intensive care unit (ICU) noted to be a demanding workplace environment, relatively little is known about the experience of doctors as they transition to intensive care medicine. Introduction: Given that guidance, literature and training on breaking bad news to < 18-year-old relatives (< 18 YOR) in an adult ICU is very limited, we surveyed critical care (CC) physicians' current practice and confidence levels surrounding this.
Methods: A Google Form investigating current practice, confidence levels, areas for development and appetite for training was disseminated to CC physicians worldwide.

As summarized in Fig. 1, visitation was lowest between 0000 and 0400 (27.3 ± 1.1 min/hour (min/hr)) and highest between 1200 and 1600 (65.5 ± 1.3 min/hr). The mean ± SE visitation spent with medical, psychiatric, and surgical patients was 51.7 ± 0.6, 38.8 ± 1.3, and 33.7 ± 3.9 min/hr respectively ( p < 0.005). Overall lowest visitation was in surgical patients between 0400 and 0800 (4.5 ± 4.5 min/hr). Introduction: During the recent COVID-19 pandemics, hospital staff often used personal protective equipment (PPE) beyond the standards recommended by the public health authorities. The aim of the study is to investigate the impact of the additional PPE compared to the standard PPE onto team performance when dealing with a medical emergency.

Methods: Single centre, prospective, randomized, controlled, openlabel, study compared 22 teams, consisting of a doctor and 2 nurses, randomized in a 1:1 ratio to use standard PPE or Super-Safe Setup in a simulated medical crisis. Before randomisation, all teams underwent a standardised mock scenario without the use of PPE was used to assess the performance at baseline. The primary outcome was Team Emergency Assessment Measure (TEAM), secondary outcomes included the timing and quality parameters of CPR and physiological changes the rescuers.

Results: As compared to standard PPE recommended by WHO [1], the use of additional PPE that included hooded coverall, significantly reduced non-technical skills of teams (TEAM score 30.6 ± 5.7 vs. 36.2 ± 5.0, p = 0.015) (Table 1), mainly due to reducing performance in complex tasks such as planning of future actions, prioritisation, and following the guidelines. This was also reflected in participants self-assessment score (Table 1). Nonetheless, there was no significant difference in the quality parameters and timing of milestones during a simulated CPR. There were no differences in rescuers physiological responses.

Conclusions: During a simulated crisis, extended PPE compared to the PPE recommended by the World Health Organisation degraded nontechnical team skills. This did not translate into measurable deterioration of patient-centred outcomes, such as quality or timing of CPR.

Introduction: Literature states a higher self-contamination rate among healthcare workers (HCWs) while doffing personal protective equipment (PPE). We aimed to compare the efficacy of this real-time RADS system against the onsite buddy system for monitoring the doffing of PPE.

Methods: This prospective, observational study was conducted at our tertiary care centre in northern India. Study was registered in the clinical trial registry India (CTRI/2020/11/038172). 200 HCWs who cared for COVID-19 patients in the intensive care units were included. Group A included HCWs who performed doffing with the help of an onsite trained observer and group B included HCWs who performed doffing with the RADS system. An independent observer noted the error at any step using the CDC doffing checklist, in both groups. An online questionnaire to analyse the level of satisfaction post-doffing was also surveyed.

Results: The proportion of errors committed during doffing was significantly lower in group B compared to group A with a low relative risk of 0.34 (95% CI 0.22-0.51) ( p < 0.001) (Fig. 1). Introduction: The critical care unit is a dynamic environment that necessitates daily clinical decision-making. Despite this, the processes and influences on decision-making have been poorly defined. Our aim was to synthesise existing research to identify factors influencing clinicians' decisions surrounding organ support.

Methods: We conducted a systematic search on three databases (PubMed, Embase and CINAHL) to find relevant papers exploring human factors that influenced decisions made by critical care clinicians. A meta-ethnography was then completed on included papers. The data were collated into a common format and cross-compared. This generated distinct themes/subthemes that were synthesised to develop a higher order interpretation.

Results: 33 studies (from 8647 citations) met the inclusion criteria. 21 of these only included nurses, 7 only doctors and 5 were interprofessional. 11 factors that influenced a clinician's decision-making were identified: experience; professional and personal risk; uncertainty; characteristics of individuals; senior support; team hierarchy; decision making by colleagues; protocols, guidelines and evidence; time and workload; hospital structure; and clinical condition. These were grouped into four themes: human, team, system and patient factors. From our interpretation of the data, we developed a model of how these themes interact to influence clinicians' decision-making (Fig. 1).

Conclusions: While decision-making surrounding organ support is complex and dynamic we identified recurring themes that influenced these decisions across different professions and environments. Further research to improve individual decision-making could be structured around addressing these themes.

Introduction: To preserve access to the intensive care unit (ICU)even in times of a shortage of critical care beds-ICUs adopt temporary measures to make room for new admissions. One measure is to transfer a patient to another ICU; a so-called 'capacity transfer' . Understanding the impact of capacity transfers on patient outcomes is of utmost importance since these transfers are not carried for the benefit of the patient. The purpose of the current study was to examine the idea that capacity transfer is associated with increased mortality compared to non-transferred patients who either died in the ICU or were discharged alive to a regular hospital ward.

Methods: In this multicentre, case-controlled, matched observational cohort study, we collected data between January 2016 and December 2019 from 68 ICUs. Capacity transferred patients were matched 1:10 using controls from the same ICU, with a stay as long or longer to avoid immortal time bias in the non-exposed population. We compared adjusted 30- and 90-day mortality rates in patients exposed to capacity transfer with non-transferred patients using potential outcomes modelling and mixed effects logistic regression modelling with propensity score adjustment.

Results: 95,909 individuals from 68 ICUs were eligible for inclusion. The main analysis group included 13,670 patients of which 1243 had been transferred due to capacity reasons. Capacity transfer was associated with a risk increase in 30-day mortality of 4.7% (95% CI 2.0-7.4; p = 0.001) compared to non-transferred patients when analysed using a potential outcomes framework (Table 1). The average risk increase in 90-day mortality was 4.9% (95% CI 2.1-7.8: p = 0.001).

Conclusions: This study demonstrates that patients undergoing capacity transfers are exposed to an increased mortality risk with about one additional death for every 20 transferred patients, which was neither caused by illness severity on admission nor by additional factors in the referring ICU.

Introduction: As part of the last two peer review processes the East of England Critical Care Network have undertaken SAQ [1] involving staff in the 18 hospitals in the region. The questionnaire is divided into 7 scales and allows a wide assessment of safety culture which has been associated with improved outcomes and reduced adverse incidents [2]. The two surveys straddle the Covid-19 pandemic which has had a recognised impact on staff welfare. We postulated that this is likely to be identifiable within the survey and wished to understand the effect on different staff groups and levels of experience.
Methods: The survey was distributed using an online platform and analysed in R.

Results: 1647 questionnaires were completed in 2019 (753) and 2022 (894). For all staff Climate scores fell significantly in all scales except stress recognition, most noticeably in job satisfaction and working conditions. Introduction: Hand hygiene observations are usually made by an observer during "office hours". Hand hygiene compliance at night/ weekends might not be comparable. Using a vest-cam (a camera attached to the shirt front) potentially allows hand hygiene compliance to be monitored at all hours of the day by retrospective analysis of the video footage. In this pilot study we present a comparison of hand hygiene observations made by an observer, versus analysis of vest-cam video taken in parallel.

Methods: Following ethics approval, 20 min observation periods were performed on ICU staff wearing a vest-cam. A human observer recorded hand hygiene opportunities (entrance and exit from the patient areas), and hand hygiene performance. The vest-cam video was analyzed by an independent observer according to the same parameters for hand hygiene opportunities and performance. The two records were then compared.

Results: Twelve observation periods were analyzed. One was excluded due to camera misplacement that resulted in the caregiver's hands not being visible. Hand hygiene performance was identified by the vest cam on 68/81 (84%) occasions versus 58/81 (72%) by the observer ( p = 0.09). Mean hand hygiene performance time was 10 ± 8 vs 11 ± 21 s ( p = 0.74). Not all hand hygiene performance was associated with defined hand hygiene opportunities. Hand hygiene events were identified on 82 occasions. All events were identified from the vestcam (82/82, 100%), while (67/82, 82%) were identified by the observer ( p < 0.001). Calculated hand hygiene compliance was similar: vest cam vs observer 51/82 (62%) versus 43/67 (64%, p = ns).

Conclusions: Analysis of video footageobtained from a shirt front mounted video camera was able to identify hand hygiene opportunities and performance at least as well as an observer. While this technique may be associated with ethical dilemmas, potentially it allows monitoring of hand hygiene compliance outside usual office hours.

Introduction: The ICU is frequently consulted when a (frail) patient critically deteriorates on a general ward. However, considering patient-tailored care, this potentially leads to the escalation of care disproportionately to the patient's pReferences, pre-existing quality of life, and functioning. Alternatively, other medical specialists, such as the palliative team, can be consulted to discuss less-invasive, comfort-based treatment options. The aim was to gain better insight into the underlying motives behind ICU consultations on general wards with a focus on (prior) documented treatment limitations (such as do-not-resuscitate, do-not-intubate, comfort-only pReferences) or for whom intensivists deem ICU treatment too invasive. Concomitantly, to explore the potential role of an earlier involvement of the palliative team in these consultations.
Methods: A qualitative study using a critical incident technique and thematic analysis.

Results: In total, 36 individual interviews were conducted between April and July 2022, with 18 ICU nurses and intensivists(in-training) consulted by general wards of a tertiary academic centre. The palliative team was involved in 6% at the time of consultation, 84% of the patients were estimated to have a life expectancy of fewer than 12 months, and 58% died within 2 months. The themes frequently discussed were awareness of the burdens of ICU treatment, establishing conformity about supervision, and timely communication about treatment limitations. Participants acknowledged the underutilization of the palliative care team due to invisibility (outside office hours) but saw a potentially valuable role in the earlier consultation of this team.

Conclusions: Although intensivists are watchful for inordinate invasive care and share responsibility for counselling or discussing treatment limitations, earlier consultation of potential other actors such as the palliative team might contribute to more patient-tailored care and more efficient use of ICU resources.

Introduction: Treatment escalation planning (TEP) is a dynamic and nuanced process, but for effective communication and handover is often summarised into a binary decision of whether or not to attempt resuscitation. Do Not Attempt Resuscitation (DNAR) status is recognised in 22 European countries [1] and in the UK, where a TEP proforma is frequently used in patient notes. The UK Guidelines for the Provision of Intensive Care Services (GPICS) states that all patients should have a treatment escalation plan documented [2], but provides little further guidance as to when it should be completed or what form it should take.

Methods: We audited TEP proforma completion on a general ICU in Cornwall, UK, and compared results to patient records that included either a proforma or narrative indices of treatment escalation planning.
Results: 21% of the patient sample had a TEP proforma. 30% had either a TEP proforma or narrative indices of a treatment escalation plan.

Conclusions: Documentation of TEP completion in this patient sample is poor and does not meet GPICS standards. Whilst narrative indices recorded in the Consultant notes were more common than TEP proformas, and likely better represent the complexity of TEP decisions while on ICU, the use of standardised proformas at time of ICU discharge contributes to more effective handover, which is crucial for ongoing care and reduction of readmission rates. Use of the proforma should serve to prompt discussion within the MDT, and with patients and their relatives to inform shared decision making. We plan to make TEP proformas mandatory at time of discharge, and reaudit in 3 months. Introduction: The discharge of patients from the intensive care unit (ICU) to a ward is a high risk transition of care [1]. The aim of this study was to identify the incidence and characteristics of patients who died in general wards after discharge from ICU.

Methods: Retrospective study of all patients discharged from a tertiary center ICU from April 2021 to October 2022. Demographic data, severity scores and hospital mortality were evaluated. Statistical analysis was performed by χ 2 and t Student tests.

Results: In this period, 715 out of 962 patients were discharged from our ICU and 55 (8%) died in the wards: 33% in the first 5 days, 18% from 6th to 10th day and 49% from 11th day on. Cause of death was: sepsis (47%), irreversible neurological injury (17%), cardiovascular disease (12%) and tracheostomy obstruction (10%). Comparing to the patients who were discharged home alive, the patients who died in the wards were older (average age 66.6 vs 58.0 years), had shorter ICU length of stay (mean 15.5 vs 23.4 days), had a higher percentage of tracheostomies (34.5 vs 14.2%), higher Charlson Comorbidity Index (3.6 vs 2.7), higher APACHE II (23.9 vs 18.9) and SAPS-II (52.8 vs 43.3) at ICU admission, higher SOFA at ICU admission (8.9 vs 7.1) and discharge (4.8 vs 2.9) and higher standardized mortality (53% vs 37%). There were no statistically significant differences concerning cause of ICU admission.

Conclusions: ICU mortality underestimates the true mortality of critically ill patients as the mortality in the first days after ICU discharge can be substantial. Though some deaths are inevitable, other are unexpected and might have been prevented by discharge to high dependence units (lacking in our hospital). In our study, deaths occurred in patients who were more likely to die: older patients with more comorbidities and higher severity scores.

Introduction: We evaluated intensivists' acceptance and understanding of Bayesian adaptive trials and explored the association between acceptance and understanding. Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) are a mainstay of medical research but have multiple drawbacks including cost and inefficiency. Bayesian adaptive trials may address these drawbacks, but are more complex and potentially less accepted by the medical community.

Methods: We surveyed United States intensivists identified from an American Medical Association email list. Participants were randomized to view an abstract describing a hypothetical Bayesian adaptive or traditional frequentist trial. The abstracts were otherwise similar in format and content with results derived from the same simulated data. Participants were then asked about self-perceived and measured understanding as well as acceptance of the trial findings. Survey results were analyzed using proportional odds logistic regression.

Results: There were 273 responses to 592 surveys (46.1%) and the groups were well balanced. The frequentist group had significantly better self-perceived ( p < 0.01 and p < 0.01) and measured understanding ( p < 0.01, p = 0.08, p < 0.01, and p = 0.04). There was no significant difference in acceptance between groups ( p = 0.47 and p = 0.10). Acceptance was significantly correlated with both self-perceived and measured understanding (Table 1). These results did not change substantially when adjusting for age, practice setting, clinical time, and subspecialty. Opinions on the increasing use of Bayesian methods were mixed: 49.5% positive, 39.2% neutral or undecided, and 11.4% negative.

Conclusions: Despite lower understanding of Bayesian adaptive trials compared to frequentist trials among intensivists we found no difference in acceptance of results. Understanding and acceptance were correlated and a high proportion of intensivists were neutral or undecided about Bayesian adaptive trials so our findings suggest further efforts to educate clinicians on these methods are warranted.

Introduction: In Canada, critical care research has traditionally been conducted in academic hospital intensive care units (ICUs). Increasing community ICUs participation (which represents two-thirds of ICU capacity in Canada) in multi-center trials may enhance recruitment, shorten time to completion and improve generalizability and quality of evidence. We aimed to identify community ICU patients that could be screened for and enrolled in large multi-center trials and quantify the potential opportunity associated with greater community ICU participation.

Methods: We first chose 10 landmark critical care trials suitable for community ICUs and extracted data on patient recruitment and study completion. We then retrospectively analyzed all patients admitted to ICU in 2018 in the province of Alberta, Canada and identified those who could have been considered for the chosen landmark trials based on their clinical characteristics. We finally performed a decision tree analysis to describe the number of patients, both in community and academic settings, that could have been eligible for participation in landmark trials. We further estimated the differences in time to completion with inclusion of community ICU patients.

Results: 10,157 adult patients were admitted to Alberta ICUs in 2018. 5650 (55.6%) were in academic centers and 4507 (44.4%) were in community hospitals. The inclusion of community ICU patients in the selected landmark critical care trials would have led on average to a 64% increase in the number of patients potentially enrolled. Furthermore, it would have decreased the mean time to completion of trials from an estimated 2.8 years with academic ICU patients only to 1.6 years (43% reduction in duration).
Conclusions: The inclusion of eligible patients admitted to community ICUs in multi-center clinical trials can accelerate recruitment and reduce time to trial completion.

abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare dexmedetomidine combined with isoflurane versus isoflurane anesthesia on brain injury after cardiac surgery. DESIGN: A prospective, randomized, single‐blind study. SETTING: University hospital. PARTICIPANTS: Adult patients undergoing elective valve replacement surgery. INTERVENTIONS: Ninety‐seven patients scheduled for valve replacement surgery were randomly divided into 2 groups: dexmedetomidine and isoflurane (Dex‐Iso, n = 50) and isoflurane alone (Iso, n = 47). Dexemedetomidine was infused at 0.6 μg/kg as a bolus, followed with 0.2 μg/kg/h until the end of surgery. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Jugular blood samples were drawn for analysis of matrix metalloproteinase‐9 (MMP‐9) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) levels on time points of: T1 (before induction); T2 (5 minutes after cardiopulmonary bypass [CPB] onset); T3 (after CPB off); T4 (the first day after operation); T5 (the second day after operation). Plasma lactate levels in arterial and jugular venous blood also were quantified. The difference between arterial and jugular bulb venous blood lactate levels (AVDL) was calculated. An antisaccadic eye movement (ASEM) test was carried out on the day before the operation and the seventh day postoperatively. In both groups, serum MMP‐9 and GFAP concentrations increased after CPB, with the peak values occurring after CPB. At time point T5, MMP‐9 and GFAP levels were close to those at T1. MMP‐9 concentrations in the Dex‐Iso group were lower than the Iso group at T3 and T4. GFAP concentrations in the Dex‐Iso group were lower at T3 but were higher than the Iso group at T2. No significant differences were found in AVDL between the 2 groups perioperatively except at T2. The ASEM scores decreased significantly postoperatively. There was no significant difference in the ASEM scores between the 2 treatment groups before and after the operation. CONCLUSIONS: The use of dexmedetomidine decreased the biochemical markers of brain injury but did not improve the neuropsychological test result after cardiac surgery.

POSTOPERATIVE BRAIN DAMAGE and neuropsychological disorders are still serious problems in cardiac surgery patients. These disorders subside within 3 to 12 months postoperatively in many cases. 1 -3 As a consequence, the

quality of life and health resources are diminished for these patients, who anticipate that postoperative improvements in physical status will generally improve their lives. Thus, the search for an ideal neuroprotective method is needed. However, the medical practice of neuroprotection remains an inexact science, owing to multifactorial mechanisms of brain injury during cardiac surgery. To date, the ideal neuroprotective treatment has not yet been found. Therefore, pharmacological agents with the potential for full neuroprotection from adverse cerebral effects have been tested. An array of anesthetics has been widely studied. However, few of them have been proven to have neuroprotective effects in clinical trials, although these bene fi ts have been demonstrated in laboratory animals. 4 -7
