Purpose: To summarize select critical care pharmacotherapy guidelines and studies published in 2016. Summary: The Critical Care Pharmacotherapy Literature Update (CCPLU) Group screened 31 journals monthly for relevant pharmacotherapy articles and selected 107 articles for review over the course of 2016. Of those included in the monthly CCPLU, three guidelines and seven primary literature studies are reviewed here. The guideline updates included are as follows: hospital-acquired pneumonia and ventilator-associated pneumonia management, sustained neuromuscular blocking agent use, and reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). The primary literature summaries evaluate the following: dexmedetomidine for delirium prevention in post-cardiac surgery, dexmedetomidine for delirium management in mechanically ventilated patients, high-dose epoetin alfa after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, ideal blood pressure targets in ICH, hydrocortisone in severe sepsis, procalcitonin-guided antibiotic de-escalation, and empiric micafungin therapy.
Conclusion: The review provides a synopsis of select pharmacotherapy publications in 2016 applicable to clinical practice.

1. Introduction

Critical care clinicians are challenged with the task of staying abreast of the medical literature in order to optimize clinical outcomes for their patients. The question of how to achieve this while attending to a busy practice is crucial with the constantly expanding body of literature. PubMed searches filtered by year using the keywords critical care and intensive care show a dramatic increase in identified publications from 5446 and 8170 in 2009 to 14,316 and 16,453 in 2016, respectively.

The Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology Section's Research Committee within the Society of Critical Care Medicine tasked a working group with creating a monthly publication in 2009 to keep its members abreast of additions to the medical literature in regards to critical care pharmacotherapy. Thus, the Critical Care Pharmacotherapy Literature Update (CCPLU), comprised of critical care pharmacists, commenced with monthly reviews of publications selected from 31 journals based on the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) system to assess quality of evidence and strength of recommendation in addition to relevance to clinical practice [1]. The monthly CCPLU is now nationally distributed electronically to a mailing group as well as via social media networks. One hundred seven articles were reviewed in 2016 with three guidelines and seven primary literature studies chosen based on their GRADE criteria (highly-rated [1A] for primary literature), their potential to change or reinforce current best practices, and an emphasis on pharmacotherapy in critical care practice.
1.1. Kalil et al. Infectious Diseases Society of America/American Thoracic Society Management of adults with hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia [2]

This guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) and ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) updated the 2005 iteration [3]. The concept of healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) was removed from the discussion in the 2016 guideline, a major change from the 2005 version. The decision to remove HCAP came from increasing evidence that suggests patients with HCAP are not at as high of a risk for multidrug-resistant organisms (MDROs) as previously considered. These guidelines suggest HCAP may be included in the upcoming community-acquired pneumonia guidelines that are anticipated to bereleased in 2017 and may define new risk factors for MDROs in HCAP.
GRADE methodology was applied to relevant articles published up to November 2015 for guideline inclusion [1]. This is the first version of the HAP and VAP guidelines to use the GRADE methodology.

Notable changes in this update are found in the newly defined risk factors for MDROs for both HAP and VAP (Table 1). These risk factors are to provide guidance in selecting empiric therapy. Other major changes for this update focused on the initial treatment of HAP and VAP. All suspected cases of HAP and VAP should be empirically covered for S. aureus , P. aeruginosa , and Gram-negative bacilli (HAP, strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence) and VAP (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). The panel determined these organisms make up the majority of HAP and VAP cases, and inadequate coverage of these organisms can lead to increased mortality. When choosing empiric treatment, a local and preferably intensive care unit (ICU)-specific antibiogram is suggested. To determine the need for empiric coverage of MDROs including methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and P. aeruginosa , it is recommended to use the defined risk factors for MDROs, severity of illness, and the local prevalence of drug-resistant organisms (Table 2).

The use of aminoglycosides as a secondary agent for the empiric treatment of VAP is not suggested if other agents with sufficient Gram-negative coverage are available for use (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence). This recommendation is supported by evidence from a meta-analysis demonstrating patients treated with or without an aminoglycoside had similar mortality rates, but those treated with an aminoglycoside had a lower clinical response rate [2,4-6]. The panel made this suggestion due to the poor lung penetration of aminoglycosides as well as the increased risk for drug-induced nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.

Patients with HAP or VAP caused by P. aeruginosa should be treated based on microbiological testing. No preferred agent was recommended due to the paucity of data pointing to a desired agent. Due to this lack of data, the use of a local antibiogram may be helpful in determining the best agent for P. aeruginosa coverage. Monotherapy is recommended for most patients with HAP or VAP caused by P. aeruginosa (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence); however, in patients with P. aeruginosa who continue to be in septic shock or at a high risk of death (i.e., mortality risk N 25%) after susceptibility results are available, continuation of two antipseudomonal antibiotics is suggested (weak recommendation, very low-quality evidence) [7-11]. This recommendation is controversial as data shows no difference in mortality, treatment failure, ICU and hospital length-of-stay (LOS), duration of mechanical ventilation or the development of resistance in patients receiving monotherapy compared to combination therapy for a HAP or VAP caused by P. aeruginosa [7,8]. The panel looked at evidence for patients in septic shock caused by P. aeruginosa from sources other than just HAP and VAP. A meta-analysis demonstrated no difference in mortality, but a propensity-matched analysis determined combination therapy was associated with a decreased mortality [9,10]. The panel felt the potential for decreased mortality outweighed the risks and burden of combination therapy.

In patients with HAP or VAP due to extended-spectrum betalactamase-producing species, antibiotic therapy should be based on antimicrobial susceptibility as well as patient-specific factors. The panel decided not to recommend an antibiotic regimen due to a lack of evidence identifying a preferable agent or combination of agents.

A preferred antibiotic regimen was suggested for the treatment of HAP or VAP due to susceptible Acinetobacter spp. with a carbapenem or ampicillin/sulbactam (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence). If the Acinetobacter is only sensitive to polymyxins, intravenous (IV) polymyxin is recommended (strong recommendation, low-quality D. Antibiotic therapy de-escalation is suggested in both HAP and VAP once susceptibilities are known (weak recommendation, very low-quality evidence).

Perhaps the most notable change to the guidelines was the recommendation for a shorter, 7-day course of antibiotic therapy regardless of organism for both HAP (strong recommendation, very low-quality evidence) and VAP (strong recommendation, moderate -quality evidence) [18-20]. No evidence exists to determine the appropriate duration of HAP therapy, which has been extrapolated from VAP data. Although there were no differences in mortality, recurrent pneumonia, treatment failure, hospital LOS, and duration of mechanical ventilation, VAP treated with shorter courses of antibiotics (i.e., 7 -8 days) was shown to increase antibiotic-free days compared with longer courses of antibiotics (i.e., 10 -15 days) [18,19]. In a subgroup analysis of patients with VAP caused by a non-glucose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus (e.g., P. aeruginosa and Acinetobacter ), patients were more likely to experience recurrence if they received a shorter course of antibiotics [20]. No difference in mortality was found between the different duration groups. In addition to the two systematic reviews, the panel's own meta-analysis of the included trials demonstrated no difference in mortality between short and long-course regimens. The panel determined even if shorter courses of antibiotics for VAP caused by non-glucose fermenting bacilli may slightly increase risk of recurrence, the patient does not seem to be at risk for increased mortality or inability to achieve a clinical cure.

Overall, the 2016 guidelines for the management of HAP and VAP introduced several major changes from the 2005 guidelines in regards to MDROriskfactors, selection of empiric therapy, and treatment duration. These suggestions were made to limit patient harm and safeguard against the superfluous use of antibiotics. To aid in this objective, a local antibiogram is suggested to optimize therapeutic regimens and de-escalate therapy. Many of the recommendations in this guideline were based on low- or very low-quality evidence, pointing to the lack of data and the pressing need for more to assist in decision-making as it relates to the management of HAP and VAP.

1.2. Murray et al. clinical practice guidelines for sustained neuromuscular blockade in the adult critically ill patient [21]

This guideline provided an update to the clinical practice guidelines regarding neuromuscular blocking agent (NMBA) use from 2002 [22]. The update broadened topics further to include information on specific indications and recommendations, clinician management of critically ill patients receiving NMBAs, mechanical ventilation management during therapy, techniques and therapies to decrease potential complications of therapy, and use in specific patient populations. A table summarizing the recommendations and the quality of evidence supporting them is provided in Table 3.

NMBA use in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) was suggested to be administered by continuous IV infusion early in its clinical course in patients with a PaO2:FiO2 b 150(weakrecommendation,moderate quality of evidence). This recommendation was supported by studies that evaluated early use of 48-hour cisatracurium infusions in adult critically ill ARDS patients [23-25]. Significant improvement in oxygenation compared to control groups was appreciated. Pooled results indicated that a 48-hour cisatracurium infusion consistently reduced risk of death at 28 days and at hospital discharge, reduced barotrauma risk, and did not increase the risk of ICU weakness [25]. The mechanism of benefit of the NMBA class in ARDS remains unknown. Regarding lung mechanics, better synchrony may lead to improved lung recruitment, ventilator compliance, systemic oxygenation, and gas exchange. These data included in the updated guidelines adjust to an evolution of findings since 2004 suggesting a reduction in inflammatory mediators, improvement in gas exchange, and improvement in 90-day mortality with use of short-term NMBAs in early ARDS. They could be considered a reasonable construct for protocolization with study methodology including ARDS criteria and ventilator settings to define patients that may benefit from early incorporation of cisatracurium, in particular.

Routine administration of NMBAs in mechanically ventilated adult patients presenting with status asthmaticus is not recommended (weak recommendation, very low quality of evidence). A trial of an NMBA is suggested in life-threatening presentations with profound hypoxemia, respiratory acidosis, or hemodynamic compromise, but the frequency of death in these patients has been retrospectively shown to be low [26-28].

The use for NMBAs in therapeutic hypothermia to manage overt shivering is suggested (weak recommendation, very low quality of evidence). Data have shown the ability for NMBAs to eliminate shivering in 100% of patients administered a therapeutic dose without a decrease in systemic blood pressure but with a decrease in oxygen consumption [29]. Potential harm of NMBAs in critically ill patients include increased risk of secondary infections including pneumonia due to increased accumulation of bronchial secretions, perpetuation of ICU-acquired weakness, decreases in blood pressure with reflexive bradycardia from autonomic ganglia blockade, and cardiovascular manifestations from histamine release from certain agents [30]. The authors do specify a good practice statement supporting a protocol-driven approach to guide NMBA administration in patients undergoing therapeutic hypothermia.

The only strong recommendation in the guidelines suggested scheduling eye care consisting of lubricating drops or gel as well as eyelid closure for patients receiving continuous infusions of NMBAs. NMBAs will result in incomplete eyelid closure and absence of corneal reflexes, which may increase the risk of developing infection, scarring, or ulcerations. These recommended therapies have been shown to reduce the prevalence of ocular surface disorders that can occur in over half of patients that are heavily sedated or receiving NMBAs, although no consensus exists on the most effective eye-care protocol [31-35].

A target blood glucose level of b 180 mg/dL in patients receiving NMBAs is recommended. Strict glycemic control has been shown to be an independent risk factor for development of critical illness polyneuromyopathy [36]. Additional data are needed to confirm this relationship in a broader population, but this remains inadequate to make specific recommendations for or against lower glucose targets [37].

It is suggested to use a consistent weight, either ideal or adjusted, when calculating NMBA doses for obese patients with a BMI exceeding 30kg/m 2 . No data are available to determine if size descriptor influences outcomes, such as LOS, when used on a sustained basis, but a common theme is recognizing the ease of ideal body weight calculation and uniformity of day-to-day endpoints.

The strength of these guidelines is in providing the most up-to-date and best evidence available regarding NMBA use, monitoring, and safety. While specific patient factors, clinical experience, and site resources should still be considered when applying these recommendations to practice or the care of individual patients, the direction provided within this document is the most comprehensive to-date. The primary weakness is that it includes many areas with no recommendation due to insufficient evidence. The authors do provide a nice review of available data within these areas to provide some guidance, but decision-making will ultimately be left up to the clinician.
1.3. Frontera et al. Neurocritical Care Society/Society of Critical Care Medicine Guideline for reversal of antithrombotics in intracranial hemorrhage [38]

These guidelines were developed through an international, multidisciplinary committee. Recommendations were established based on available clinical trials, meta-analyses, pre-clinical studies, review articles, and practice guidelines through November 2015. The quality of evidence and strength of recommendations were presented using the GRADE system, which allows for ' strong ' or ' conditional ' recommendations with supportive evidence described as high, moderate, low or very low. ' Good practice statements ' are used to imply high confidence in recommendations taken from indirect evidence where a formal GRADEassessmentwould bechallenging to complete [39]. A table summarizing the recommendations can be found in Table 4.

Urgent vitamin K antagonist (VKA) reversal with vitamin K and prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is recommended in patients with intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Vitamin K administration results in sustained reversal of anticoagulant activity; however, reduction of INR to b 1.4 has been shown to take up to 24 h [40-42]. A retrospective study found intra-parenchymal hemorrhage growth in 50% of patients receiving vitamin K alone compared to 33% and 19% in patients receiving fresh frozen plasma(FFP) and PCC, respectively [43]. Delay in VKA reversal in the setting of ICH may worsen outcomes; therefore, vitamin K therapy is only recommended in combination with other reversal agents.

Three- or four-factor PCCs are recommended for VKA reversal in ICH over FFP (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). VKA reversal with FFP has been shown to be effective but delayed when compared to PCC [44]. In one study, FFP was retrospectively associated with a higher risk of major hemorrhage and increased risk of death or severe disability at three months compared to PCC [45]. Administration of PCC for VKA-associated ICH results in a more rapid INR reversal compared to FFP alone; however, data evaluating functional outcomes are conflicting [46,47]. Administration of FFP is recommended if PCC are unavailable (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Four-factor PCC is recommended over three-factor PCC based on evidence from a systematic review indicating a more rapid INR reversal and the theoretical benefit of inclusion of Factor VII (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence) [48].

Direct factor Xa inhibitors have relatively short elimination half-lives and cessation of drug therapy may be sufficient management for minor bleeding [49]. Guidance of pharmacologic strategy for reversal should be based on timing of last drug exposure (Good Practice Statement) and presence of bleeding over laboratory data (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence). Administration of activated charcoal is recommended if presentation occurs within 2hofdrugexposure(conditionalrecommendation,very low quality evidence). Effectiveness of activated charcoal may be limited in rivaroxaban, as rivaroxaban is not bound by charcoal and undergoes rapid gastric absorption. Activated charcoal should be reserved for patients with low risk for aspiration who present immediately after drug administration [50]. A murine model evaluating reversal of rivaroxaban in the setting of intra-parenchymal hematoma found administration of four factor PCC, FFP, and activated recombinant factor seven (rFVIIa) each prevented hematoma expansion but no therapy completely corrected prothrombin time [51]. Although data are limited, administration of four-factor PCC or activated PCC (aPCC) is recommended if ICH occurs within 3 -5terminal half-lives of drug administration (conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence) and is recommended over rFVIIa due to lower risk for thrombosis (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence). Targeted reversal therapies for direct factor Xa inhibitors including andexanet alfa and ciraparantag are being evaluated for efficacy and are not currently approved by the Food and Drug Administration.

Initial recommended management for direct thrombin inhibitor (DTI) associated ICH includes discontinuation of the antithrombotic agent and assessment of last known drug administration time, renal function, and drug interactions (Good Practice Statement). Similar to direct factor Xa inhibitors, cessation of DTI agents may be sufficient management in the setting of non-life threatening hemorrhage depending on the half-life of the specific DTI agent. Evidence from one study evaluating dabigatran patients with intracranial hemorrhage found no hematoma growth after discontinuation of dabigatran; however, time from last dose was not reported. Generally, there is no role for administration of reversal agents N 3 -5 half-lives from the last known drug administration time as the remaining antithrombotic effects are likely negligible in the absence of renal insufficiency [52].

Activated charcoal may be considered for reversal of oral DTI agents if the last known drug exposure occurred within 2 h of presentation and risk for aspiration is low (conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence). Idarucizumab is a monoclonal antibody fragment that neutralizes dabigatran and is recommended first line for dabigatran reversal if the last known dose occurred within 3 -5 half-lives (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence) or if renal insufficiency is present resulting in prolonged drug exposure beyond 3 -5 half-lives (strong recommendation, moderate quality evidence). Idarucizumab has been shown to completely reverse dabigatran-induced coagulopathy within 4 h of administration [53]. Re-anticoagulation secondary to redistribution of dabigatran from the extravascular to the intravascular space may occur; therefore, re-dosing of idarucizumab is recommended if clinically significant bleeding persists after initial treatment (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence). Four-factor PCC or aPCC are recommended for DTI reversal in the setting of ICH if idarucizumab is not available or if the ICH is associated with a DTI other than dabigatran (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence). Animal and healthy volunteer studies have suggested PCC may correct dabigatraninduced coagulopathy; however, a prospective cross-over in vivo study found four-factor PCC did not correct dabigatran-induced changes in thrombin time, endogenous thrombin potential, ecarin clotting time, or activated partial thromboplastin time [54,55]. Conversely, a small case series of patients with dabigatran-associated life-threatening hemorrhage described adequate hemostasis after administration of aPCC [56,57]. Additional dosing of reversal agents should be based on evidence for clinically significant bleeding over laboratory parameters (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence).

Hemodialysis is recommended for patients with dabigatran-related ICH and renal insufficiency when idarucizumab is not available or clinically significant bleeding is still present after reversal (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence). Dabigatran is removed by hemodialysis and studies have shown effective drug clearance in both intermittent and continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration [58-60]. There is insufficient evidence to support rFVIIa and FFP for DTI reversal; therefore, these agents are not recommended (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Recommendations for the reversal of direct oral anticoagulants aligned with the guidance document from the International Society on Thrombosis and Hemostasis [61].

There is no targeted reversal agent available for low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) agents, and data vary regarding the efficacy of protamine sulfate for LMWH reversal in the setting of active hemorrhage. A small case series (n = 14) found protamine sulfate administration halted hemorrhage expansion in 64% of patients receiving therapeutic enoxaparin, whereas a separate case report described continued intracranial hemorrhage despite protamine sulfate administration [62,63]. Protamine sulfate administration may lead to incomplete reversal of LMWH agents. Specifically, anti-Xa activity may not be adequately neutralized [64]. Given the lack of available targeted reversal

Case reports indicate rFVIIa may be efficacious for LMWH reversal; however, this must be weighed against the increased risk for thrombosis [65-72]. The authors recommend rFVIIa administration for LMWH reversal only if protamine sulfate is contraindicated (conditional recommendation, very low quality evidence). Antithrombotic effects of pentasaccharide agents are not reversed by protamine sulfate [74]. PCC and aPCC have been shown in vitro and in animal studies to correct fondaparinux-induced coagulopathy [75,76]. One retrospective study evaluating various reversal treatments in acute coronary or venous thromboembolism patients treated with fondaparinux who experienced a 10% reduction in hematocrit described hemostasis attributed to rFVIIa in 50% of patients [74]. Multiple studies identified superior normalization of laboratory values and reduced bleeding time for aPCC compared to rFVIIa; therefore, aPCC is recommended for reversal of pentasaccharide agents in the setting of ICH (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence) [76,77]. rFVIIa is recommended if aPCC is contraindicated or unavailable (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence).

Cryoprecipitate is recommended for reversal of symptomatic ICH if a thrombolytic agent was administered in the last 24 h (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence). Outcome-related data to support this recommendation are sparse, and multiple studies have found no difference in functional outcome or mortality [78,79]. Cryoprecipitate is recommended over FFP due to lower required transfusion volumes (no GRADE assessment provided). Limited data are available that evaluate the utilization of antifibrinolytic agents for thrombolytic reversal; however, a single case report of tranexamic acid administration in alteplase-associated ICH described no hematoma expansion [79]. Despite the lack of available data, antifibrinolytic agents are recommended as an alternative to cryoprecipitate (conditional recommendation, very lowquality evidence). The role of platelet transfusions for the reversal of thrombolytic agents in the setting of ICH is unclear based on the results of a multi-center, retrospective study describing an association with increased hematoma expansion [78].

Reversal of antiplatelet agents in the setting of ICH is controversial as the impact of such agents on hematoma expansion and other clinical outcomes is largely unknown [80 -83]. One randomized controlled trial evaluated platelet transfusion compared to no transfusion in patients with acute hypertensive basal ganglia hemorrhage undergoing neurosurgical intervention. The authors found less hemorrhage recurrence, lower post-operative hematoma volume, and lower mortality in the platelet transfusion group [84]. The external validity of this study has been questioned given the single-center design, and the results may be difficult to interpret as various sub-groups may increase the risk for type-1 error. A prospective observational study found platelet transfusions led to smaller follow-up hemorrhage and increased the likelihood of a modified Rankin score less than four in intraparenchymal hemorrhage patients with abnormal platelet function [85]. The PATCH trial was a randomized controlled trial comparing platelet transfusion compared to standard of care in patients on antiplatelet therapy with spontaneous ICH [86]. Patients in the platelet transfusion group had significantly higher odds of death or dependence at 90 days; therefore, the authors concluded platelet transfusion was inferior to standard care in patients taking antiplatelet therapy who experience ICH. Based on available prospective evidence, multiple retrospective studies showing no clinical impact of platelet transfusion, and the increased risk for adverse events associated with transfusion, platelet transfusion is only recommended in aspirin- or adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitor-associated ICH patients who will undergo neurosurgical intervention (conditional recommendation, moderate quality evidence).

Desmopressin (DDAVP) administration has a low risk for adverse events and has been found to improve platelet function in ICH patients [87,88]. As a result, DDAVP is recommended in ICH associated with aspirin/COX-1 inhibitors, ADP receptor inhibitors, and in addition to platelet transfusion in patients undergoing neurosurgical intervention (conditional recommendation, low quality evidence).

Antithrombotic use is increasing as the prevalence of pro-thromboembolic disease states such as atrial fibrillation rise [89 -91]. The reviewed guideline recommendations address an increasing patient population at risk for devastating ICH. Concise, evidenced-based recommendations for the reversal of antithrombotic agents in the setting of ICH may assist practitioners to expedite emergent treatment. This guideline provides more specific guidance for reversal agent dosing compared to the 2015 American Heart Association (AHA)/American Stroke Association (ASA) recommendations for the management of spontaneous intracranial hemorrhage [92]. The scope of this guideline is limited to adult patients and does not address considerations for special populations including pediatrics, geriatrics, or those presenting with complex clinical scenarios. Unfortunately, this guideline failed to produce strong recommendations for reversal of all reviewed antithrombotic agents. This limitation is secondary to a lack of high quality data or available targeted reversal agent.

Secondary outcomes included distribution of each CPC level at post-arrest days 30 and 60 in addition to all-cause mortality during ICU stay, hospital stay, at day 30, and at day 60. Additionally, adverse events were monitored through day 60.

Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, including time from collapse to ROSC (median 25 min in both groups, p = 0.57) and incidence of targeted temperature management (93.5% of all cases). Median time to first dose of epoetin alfa was 1.43 h (IQR 0.8 -2.7). Due to the high incidence of early mortality, only 75.6% of patients randomized received the entire 48-hour treatment course.

There were no differences between groups in the primary outcome at 60 days (epoetin alfa: 32.4% vs. control: 32.1%; OR 1.01; 95% CI 0.68 -1.48; p = 0.96). Furthermore, distribution of CPC at every level wassimilar between groups at all time points. Mortality rate was similar at all time points, with 57.7% and 56.4% of patients being alive at 60 days in the epoetin alfa and control groups, respectively (p = 0.85). Anoxic brain injury was the primary cause of death in both groups, accounting for 76.9% and 78.2% of patients in the epoetin alfa and control cohorts, respectively (p = 0.74). Serious adverse events were more frequently observed in the epoetin alfa group compared to the control group (22.6% vs. 14.9%; p = 0.03), including an increased risk of thromboembolic complications (12.4% vs. 5.8%; p = 0.01).

Anoxo-ischemic injury remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality following cardiac arrest, with targeted temperature management as the only intervention that has demonstrated improved outcomes [97,98]. Despite preliminary data suggesting that erythropoietin analogs may provide neurocognitive protection, this present study failed to demonstrate benefit and found a risk of increased complications. Animal models demonstrated erythropoietin- induced neuronal and vascular protection in the nervous system, thus it has been investigated in a variety of clinical scenarios, including acute myocardial infarction, middle cerebral aneurysm stroke, and traumatic brain injury [99 -105]. In a single-center feasibility study, epoetin alfa did not impact survival rates in 18 patients compared to 40 patients in a matched cohort; however, neurological recovery was higher (55% vs. 37.5%; p N 0.05) [106]. Another single-center study suggested that erythropoietin-beta administration within 2 min of cardiopulmonary resuscitation results in a higher rate of ROSC, ICU admission, and survival to discharge [107]. Contrary to these previously documented positive studies, the current study failed to replicate these single center results in a multicenter format.

In experimental models, the therapeutic window varied, but was observed up until 3 h. Although the median time to administration was 1.5 h, it is possible that the time window was missed. The dosage chosen of 200,000 units over a 48hour period was the highest studied dose and twice the dose used in stroke patients, thus it likely achieved adequate concentrations [101, 102]. This study was initiated prior to the revision of the consensus definitions of ' sepsis ' and ' septic shock ' and also prior to the publication of the 2016 Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) guidelines. Because of this, the terms ' severe sepsis ' and ' septic shock ' in this study were based upon the definitions from the 2012 SSC guidelines [134 -136]. In addition, the 2016 SSC guidelines utilized the term ' sepsis ' for the patients in the HYPRESS study that were in the ' severe sepsis ' group [137]. Patients in the treatment group received a hydrocortisone taper that started with a 50 mg IV bolus followed by a 24-hour continuous infusion consisting of 200 mg on days 1 to 5, 100 mg on days 6 and 7, 50 mg on days 8 and 9, and 25 mg on days 10 and 11. Hydrocortisone was given as a continuous infusion following the recommendations in the 2012 SSC guidelines and tapered according to the recommendations in the CORTICUS trial [134, 135]. The primary outcome was the progression from severe sepsis to septic shock within 14 days. Patients were evaluated daily for the developmentof septic shock for up to 14 days or until discharge from the ICU. Secondary outcomes included time until septic shock, ICU or hospital mortality, survival up to 180 days, assessment of secondary infections, weaning failure, muscle weakness and hyperglycemia.

A total of 380 patients were randomized (190 per group), with 353 analyzed in the intention-to-treat analysis. The baseline characteristics including organ dysfunction, source of infection, and glucocorticoid use prior to ICU admission were similar between both groups.

Regarding the primary infectious etiology, there was less pneumonia and more thoracic, intra-abdominal, and catheter-related infections in the hydrocortisone group, compared to the placebo group (p N 0.05). There was no significant difference in the treatment groups regarding progression to the primary endpoint of septic shock. In the intentionto-treat population, septic shock occurred in 36 of 170 patients (21.2%) in the hydrocortisone group compared to 39 of 170 patients (22.9%) in the placebo group (difference -1.8%; 95% CI -10.7 -+7.2%; p = 0.70). In the per-protocol population, septic shock occurred in 29 of 155 patients (18.7%) in the hydrocortisone group compared to 33 of 156 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (difference -2.4%; 95% CI -11.5 -+6.6; p = 0.59). Subgroup analyses evaluating medical, surgical, pneumonia patients, or treatment with study medication for 48 h showed no benefit for prevention of septic shock.

The HYPRESS study is the first to investigate whether the use of hydrocortisone in patients with severe sepsis will prevent progression to septic shock. There have been many studies conducted that have investigated the use of steroids in various stages of sepsis and septic shock and several reviews of the medical literature evaluating those studies andtheir outcomes. The quality of evidence of these studies and the outcomes has been mixed. The recommendations from the recent 2016 SSC guidelines are to treat septic shock with hydrocortisone only in adult patients who have not had an adequate response to fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy [137]. The 2016 SSC guideline specifically references the HYPRESS study and states that steroids should not be used in septic patients to prevent septic shock. Use of hydrocortisone as investigated in this study is not recommended in severe sepsis and only in specific clinical situations in septic shock (e.g. history of steroid therapy or adrenal dysfunction). Furthermore, this study concluded that in adult patients with severe sepsis, the use of hydrocortisone showed no difference in incidence of patients progressing to septic shock within 14 days. Based upon the HYPRESS study results and the recommendations of the most recent SSC guidelines, hydrocortisone for severe sepsis to prevent the progression to septic shock is not clinically indicated.
2. Conclusion
The review provides a synopsis of select pharmacotherapy publications in 2016 applicable to critical care practice.

Editor d Recent studies 1,2 have not supported the hypothesis that perioperative dexmedetomidine improves outcomes from cardiac surgery via sympatholytic, anti-inflammatory or organ-protective effects. 3 Postoperative delirium has been a key area of recent interest. Two recent high-profile studies have not found significant effects on this endpoint, but show trends to effects on mortality. 1,2 Notably, the lack of effect on delirium may be attributable to over-sedation in one trial, evident by prolonged ventilation time in the dexmede tomidine-treated group. 2 That study 2 used methods that are excellent for detecting delirium in ventilated patients but suboptimal for non-intubated patients, 4 consistent with the low overall delirium rates detected. The other study 1 included both the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) and CAM-ICU, which is a more comprehensive approach to delirium assessment. However, this study also showed no overall effects on in-hospital delirium but a trend to reduced delirium in the ICU. 1 This more short-term effect is likely more biologically plausible, but was not statistically proven. Intriguingly the study by Momeni and colleagues 1 suggested a potentially large effect on in-hospital mortality with 10-fold lower mortality in the dexmedetomidine group (for which the authors offer an appropriately conservative interpretation).

As the delirium results seemed inconsistent with prior literature, and the mortality effects seemed surprisingly large, we conducted a hypothesis-generating meta-analysis of the available data from RCTs (based on other recent meta-analyses 5,6 updated with new studies 1,7 ). The meta-analysis was performed in R with the package 'metafor ' (R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). Odds ratios were calculated for each article included in the analysis based on the incidence of delirium and mortality events from the total. Arandom effects model was fit to each outcome (delirium and mortality) both separately and combined.

Our updated meta-analysis shows that delirium after cardiac surgery is reduced by 46% (odds ratio 0.54 [95% confidence interval 0.38 e 0.76]), however 30-day in-hospital mortality is not significantly reduced (odds ratio 0.55 [95% confidence interval 0.27 e 1.13], Fig. 1). We propose that 'days alive and at home ' would be a reasonable patient-centred outcome for such a study that captures meaningful morbidity (such as delirium) and mortality. 8 Given that delirium and mortality risk are elevated in older subjects, and secondary analysis of the 4000 patient SPICE III trial suggested a specific benefit of dexmedetomidine sedation in older, surgical, or both participants, 9 such a trial should focus on vulnerable older patients. We suggest that because of design limitations, current trial data do not address the important question of potential benefits of early perioperative administration of dexmedetomidine in cardiac surgical ICU patients. Future studies should address the potential benefit of sympatholytic, organ-protective dosing of dexmedetomidine during and after surgery, as intraoperative administration may offer particular benefits. 10,11

Editor d We thank Hu and colleagues 1 for their interest in our study on the perioperative use of dexmedetomidine in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, in which we showed that dexmedetomidine infusion (initiated from cardiopulmonary bypass until tracheal extubation or 24 h) was associated with reduced death up to 5 yr after cardiac surgery. 2 We initially found a higher 5-yr survival rate in patients who received dexmedetomidine compared with those who did not in the original unadjusted cohort of 2068 patients. After adjustment for baseline covariates using propensity score matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting, or overlap weighting techniques, this association between dexmedetomidine use and long-term survival remained. In Figure 1, a graphic summary of dexmedetomidine's effect on survival after cardiac surgery is shown for a better demonstration of our study findings.

Hu and colleagues 1 suggest that several contraindications of dexmedetomidine use (including heart rate > 120 beats min [UNMAPPED_GLYPH U+0000] 1 , severe sinus bradycardia, secondor third-degree atrioventricular block, or sick sinus syndrome) should be incorporated into the exclusion criteria of our study. First, there is no absolute contraindication to the use of dexmedetomidine, but it should be used with caution in patients with bradycardia and hypotension. 3,4 Second, our inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied during the screening process of electronic medical records and our institutional Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) National Adult Cardiac Surgery Database. Third, whether patients received perioperative dexmedetomidine was at the discretion of the attending anaesthesiologists such that we are unable to decide who would receive dexmedetomidine or not.

Their second suggestion is to include details of the diagnosis of heart block after surgery. We did present the definitions of postoperative outcomes in Supplementary Table S1 of our article. Based on the STS national criteria, heart block was defined as new heart block requiring implantation of a permanent pacemaker of any type before hospital discharge. 5 Thus, only new onset heart block that was treated with permanent pacemaker implantation was recorded. Here, we would like to reiterate that multiple testing was not planned for the secondary outcomes (including the incidence of postoperative complications and utilisation of healthcare resources), so we are not able to draw any definite clinical inference from these secondary outcomes.

abstract: OBJECTIVE: The aim of our study was to compare the clinical effects of sedation with dexmedetomidine vs. propofol in patients undergoing cardiac surgery and analyze their effects on the duration of mechanical ventilation (MV), length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU), and total hospital stay. PATIENTS AND METHODS: The study included 120 patients who were randomized in a 1:1 ratio into two groups of 60 patients. The first group was sedated with continuous dexmedetomidine in doses 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h. The second group was sedated with propofol in doses 1-2 mg/kg/h. RESULTS: Patients sedated with dexmedetomidine required 2.2 hours less time on MV (p<0.001). There was a positive correlation between the duration of MV and the ICU length of stay (r=0.368; p<0.001), as well as between the duration of MV and the total hospital stay (r=0.204; p=0.025). Delirium occurred in the postoperative period in 25% of patients sedated with propofol, while in the dexmedetomidine group it was only 11.7% (p=0.059). Patients who developed delirium had a significantly longer duration of MV (12.6±5.4 vs. 9.3±2.5 hours, p=0.010). CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative sedation with dexmedetomidine, compared to propofol, reduces the duration of MV, but does not influence the length of stay in the ICU and length of hospitalization after open heart surgery.

Abstract. - OBJECTIVE: The aim of our study was to compare the clinical effects of sedation with dexmedetomidine vs. propofol in patients undergoing cardiac surgery and analyze their effects on the duration of mechanical ventilation (MV), length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU), and total hospital stay.

PATIENTS AND METHODS: The study included 120 patients who were randomized in a 1:1 ratio into two groups of 60 patients. The first group was sedated with continuous dexmedetomidine in doses 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h. The second group was sedated with propofol in doses 1-2 mg/kg/h.

RESULTS: Patients sedated with dexmedetomidine required 2.2 hours less time on MV ( p <0.001). There was a positive correlation between the duration of MV and the ICU length of stay ( r =0.368; p <0.001), as well as between the duration of MV and the total hospital stay ( r =0.204; p =0.025). Delirium occurred in the postoperative period in 25% of patients sedated with propofol, while in the dexmedetomidine group it was only 11.7% ( p =0.059). Key Words:
Dexmedetomidine, Mechanical ventilation, Cardiac surgery, Postoperative delirium, Sedation.
Introduction

According to the lately developed Early Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) concept 1 , one of the main goals of the postoperative strategy is earlier extubation and a shorter duration of mechanical ventilation (MV) with adequate sedation. Patients undergoing open heart surgery should be on MV and sedated from one to six hours after surgery 1,2 . Prolonged MV is associated with numerous complications, eventually leading to longer stay in the intensive care unit (ICU), longer hospital stay, and higher morbidity and mortality. This can cause permanent harm, disadvantages, and loss of independence. Apart from the impeded health and disrupted quality of life of both patients and their families, this leads to higher treatment costs and increases the economic burden 1,3-5 .

Sedation during MV enables the patient's synchronization with the ventilator, prevents agitation, reduces hemodynamic instability, and reduces subjective discomfort6. Specific measures are recommended to reduce the duration of sedation and MV, improve outcomes and reduce complications in ICU patients 6,7 . These include the selection of an adequate sedative, daily sedation interruption, and spontaneous breathing trials. Dexmedetomidine and propofol are the most widely used sedatives with distinct pharmacological features that make them suitable for sedation after cardiac surgery 4,8-11 .

Dexmedetomidine is a potent α2 agonist with anxiolytic, sedative, analgesic, and sympatholytic effects. Continuous dexmedetomidine infusion causes hypnosis and sedation without respiratory depression, so it can provide earlier postoperative extubation and prevent blood oxygen level variations 1,3,4,12 . Due to the analgesic effect, dexmedetomidine use reduces the need for opioids 13,14 .

[DOCLING_PAGE 2]
Dexmedetomidine vs. propofol sedation after cardiac surgery
The most common side effects 8,9,14 of dexmedetomidine include bradycardia and hypotension, which are attributed to the sympatholytic effect.

Propofol has represented the gold standard for sedation after cardiac surgery for decades, due to the rapid onset of action, fast recovery after discontinuation, and relatively low cost. Nonetheless, its use has been restricted due to common hemodynamic instability and respiratory depression, observed even with regular doses of propofol 3,8,13-16 .

The aim of the present study was to compare the clinical effects of sedation with dexmedetomidine vs. propofol in patients undergoing cardiac surgery, and analyze their effects on the duration of MV, length of stay in the ICU, and total hospital stay.
Patients and Methods

This was a prospective, randomized, single-blinded, controlled clinical trial. The study was conducted at the Clinic for Cardiovascular Surgery of the Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases Vojvodina between 01 March 2022 and 30 September 2022. The study protocol complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases Vojvodina. Informed consent was obtained from all individual participants included in the study. The study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05849597).
Study Population

The study included patients of both sexes scheduled for elective cardiac surgery with the use of cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) (including coronary artery bypass grafting, valve repair/replacement, and combined). The study included adult patients, older than 18 years, with a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) >40%. Patients with preoperative atrial fibrillation, previous history of interventionally treated arrhythmias, second- and third-degree atrioventricular block, bradycardia with heart rate ≤50/min, pacemaker, renal or hepatic insufficiency, or undergoing emergency procedures were excluded from the study. Patients with a history of serious mental illness, delirium, and severe dementia were excluded as well.

A total of 620 patients were screened, of whom 465 were excluded due to exclusion criteria, and 30 declined to participate in the study. From 125 patients that were selected, 5 patients subsequently requested to be excluded from the study (Figure 1).

After inclusion, all the patients filled in an epidemiological questionnaire which included general and demographic data, and information about alcohol and cigarette consumption. Blood laboratory analyses and hemodynamic parameters were recorded for all the patients as well.
Anesthesia and CPB Management

Anesthesia was induced with combination of sufentanil, midazolam, propofol, and rocuronium bromide. After intubation, the lungs were mechanically ventilated with an oxygen/air mixture of 50:50. Anesthesia was maintained with sevoflurane, analgesia with a continuous infusion of sufentanil, and muscle relaxation with intermittent administration of rocuronium bromide. Perioperative and postoperative monitoring included continuous arterial and central venous pressure measurement, electrocardiography (ECG), oxygen saturation (pulse oximetry), body temperature measured in the nasopharynx, and diuresis. Arterial blood gas analyses were performed intermittently. The heart rate and blood pressure were maintained within 25% of the baseline values. Anticoagulation was achieved with heparin to maintain an activated clotting time above 480 s.

Management of CPB included mild hypothermia (32-34°C) and targeted mean perfusion pressure between 60 and 80 mmHg. Myocardial protection was achieved with antegrade intermittent cold (extracellular crystalloid or blood) cardioplegia. Before separation from CPB, patients were rewarmed to 36° to 37°C. After separation from CPB, heparin was neutralized with protamine sulfate, 1 mg/100 U heparin, to achieve an activated clotting time under 130 s. All patients were transferred to the ICU after completing surgery.
Study Design

All 120 patients included in the study were randomized in 1:1 ratio, using computer-generated numbers, into two groups of 60 patients. Upon arrival at the ICU, vital parameters were measured. The first group of patients was sedated with continuous dexmedetomidine infusion in doses 0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h. Dexmedetomidine infusion was discontinued before weaning from MV and extubation. For patients requiring MV longer than 24 hours, dexmedetomidine infusion was substituted with propofol. The second group of patients was sedated with continuous propofol infusion in doses 1-2 mg/kg/h. Propofol infusion was also discontinued before weaning from MV and extubation.

Figure 1. Flow diagram of the study.

The sedation level was assessed using the Richmond Agitation and Sedation Scale (RASS) every two hours. Postoperative analgesia was managed according to the protocol (opioid analgesics, non-steroid anti-inflammatory drugs, paracetamol), with pain level assessment using a visual analog scale (0 - no pain; 10 - unbearable pain).

The following data were observed: age, sex, body mass index (BMI), hemoglobin, heart rate, and LVEF. Among the postoperative parameters, the following were analyzed: duration of MV (in hours), extubation time, ICU and hospital length of stay (in days), postoperative hemoglobin, blood product transfusion rates, occurrence of atrial fibrillation, and assessment of delirium. Assessment of delirium was performed using the confusion assessment method for ICU (CAM-ICU) every 12 hours during five postoperative days.
Statistical Analysis

At the moment of trial design, on the basis of previously published literature, we assumed an average duration (12.8 hours) of MV in patients after open heart surgery with standard sedation. The recruitment of 109 patients with 1:1 randomization was required for a significant reduction in the duration of MV to provide a power of 80% with α=0.05.

Continuous variables were expressed as arithmetic mean ± standard deviation, while categorical variables were expressed as absolute numbers and percentages. Two groups were compared using the independent samples t -test or Mann-Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the Chi-square test for categorical variables. Statistical significance for all of the tests was set at the p -value <0.05. All the analyses were performed using SPSS, version 20.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).
[DOCLING_PAGE 4]
Dexmedetomidine vs. propofol sedation after cardiac surgery
Results

There were no significant differences between dexmedetomidine and propofol group in age and gender distribution and other baseline characteristics (Table I). Both dexmedetomidine and propofol groups had similar preoperative hemoglobin levels (135.8±15.7 vs. 131.1±16.1 g/l, p =0.112), heart rate (68.1±10.6 vs. 70.6±12.7 bpm, p =0.236), and left ventricular ejection fraction (57.3±6.6 vs. 57.7±6.6 %, p =0.780). CPB time (69.2±26.9 vs. 76.6±27.5 min; p =0.143) and aortic cross-clamp time (59.9±23.7 vs. 66.3±24.4 min; p =0.144) were similar in dexmedetomidine and propofol group.

Patients sedated with dexmedetomidine required 2.2 hours shorter time on MV compared to patients sedated with propofol, which represents a 20% reduction ( p <0.001) (Figure 2). There were two patients in the propofol group who required mechanical ventilation beyond 24 hours, while there were no such patients in the dexmedetomidine group.

There was a significant positive correlation between the duration of MV and the ICU length of stay ( r =0.368; p <0.001), as well as between the duration of MV and the total hospital length of stay ( r =0.204; p =0.025). There was no significant correlation between CPB time ( r =0.053; p =0.566) and aortic cross-clamp time ( r =0.063; p =0.494) with the duration of MV.

The length of stay in the ICU was 1 day for the majority of patients in both groups, and the total hospital stay was slightly over 7 days for both groups (Table II). There were no patients with fatal outcomes in either group.

Delirium in the postoperative period assessed with the CAM-ICU score was observed in one-quarter of patients sedated with propofol, while patients sedated with dexmedetomidine experienced delirium only half as much. Although the level of significance was slightly beyond the threshold ( p =0.059), the difference is indi cative. Patients who developed delirium had a significantly longer duration of MV (12.6±5.4 vs. 9.3±2.5 hours, p =0.010) (Figure 3).
The two groups had a similar number of patients with new-onset atrial fibrillation, as well as patients requiring red blood cell transfusions in the postoperative period (Table II).
Discussion

The current study is a prospective randomized clinical trial confirming that dexmedetomidine-based postoperative sedation reduces the duration of MV after open heart surgery in compared to sedation with propofol. Our results demonstrated that longer MV is associated with longer stays in the ICU, more postoperative hospital days, and increased incidence of postoperative delirium in patients after cardiac surgery.

MV of the lungs represents an integral part of the postoperative recovery after cardiac surgery. Leaving behind the concept of opioid anesthesia has enabled faster postoperative recovery and earlier weaning from MV and extubation. Today, the majority of patients after cardiac surgery are extubated within 6 hours after surgery. However, 6-20% of patients require prolonged MV 17,18 , which is associated with higher morbidity and mortality, increased length of stay in the ICU, longer total hospital stay, worse quality of life and higher economic burden 19,20 .

Factors influencing the length of postoperative MV include the patient's preoperative condition, comorbidities, type of cardiac surgery, and type of anesthesia. Nevertheless, recovery after surgery is also influenced by the selection of medications used for postoperative sedation. Sedation based on benzodiazepines was used as a standard globally up until 2018. Due to the extended sedative effects, benzodiazepines were associated with prolonged MV and longer stays in the ICU. Their use was also associated with a higher incidence of postoperative delirium 21 .

Sedation, Delirium, Immobility and Sleep Disruption in Adult Patients in the Intensive care unit (ICU) 22 recommended the use of dexmedetomidine and propofol, instead of benzodiazepines, for sedation in mechanically ventilated patients. Both dexmedetomidine and propofol are two shortacting agents that are widely used. Although both of them are first-line agents, there are only few studies in literature directly comparing their effects and outcomes in patients after cardiac surgery.

A recently published large retrospective study by Hu et al 20 included 1,388 patients after coronary artery bypass graft surgery. The authors demonstrated that patients sedated with dexmedetomidine had fewer postoperative respiratory complications and a shorter duration of MV compared to propofol, which is similar to what we observed in our study. Hu et al20 also showed shorter stay in the ICU and shorter hospital stay in the group of patients sedated with dexmedetomidine. In contrast, our results did not show a difference in the time spent in the ICU and total hospital stay. This can be explained by the local practice of our hospital to discharge the patients without serious complications of open-heart surgery from the ICU on the first postoperative day. This is important because transferring patients to regular departments enables them better day-night rhythm, noise reduction, earlier mobilization, and the ability to feed themselves and take care of personal hygiene. Most importantly, this provides early contact with family and their inclusion in the patients' recovery. Furthermore, our local practice is to discharge patients home routinely on the sixth postoperative day after open heart surgery if they are recovering well and their postoperative course is uneventful. This enables them to return to their families, familiar surroundings and daily activities as soon as possible. Evidence clearly demonstrates that all of these methods represent crucial measures for the prevention of postoperative delirium and can reduce postoperative morbidity and mortality 23-28 .
[DOCLING_PAGE 6]
Dexmedetomidine vs. propofol sedation after cardiac surgery

Another retrospective study published by Wanat et al 4 also demonstrated a shorter duration of MV in patients sedated with dexmedetomidine after cardiac surgery. The explanation for such results most probably lies in the fact that dexmedetomidine does not cause respiratory depression. Also, due to the analgesic effect of dexmedetomidine, the patients require fewer opioids, which further reduces respiratory depression. Additionally, dexmedetomidine expresses a favorable hemodynamic profile 29 . In contrast, propofol significantly lowers arterial blood pressure through the reduction in cardiac output and vasodilation 15 . Furthermore, dexmedetomidine suppresses pulmonary oxidative stress and inflammatory response, thus reducing the severity of acute lung injury induced by the remote organ ischemia-reperfusion 30,31 . Similar to our results, the aforementioned study by Wanat et al 4 did not demonstrate a difference between dexmedetomidine and propofol sedation in the ICU length stay and total hospital stay.

On the contrary, a randomized controlled trial by Eremenko and Chemova 32 , who also compared the effects of dexmedetomidine and propofol for postoperative sedation after cardiac surgery, failed to show the difference in the duration of postoperative MV. Nevertheless, they did demonstrate a significantly shorter length of stay in the ICU in the dexmedetomidine group. Although the dexmedetomidine dose range used for sedation was the same as in our study (0.2-0.7 mcg/kg/h), we generally used minimal doses of dexmedetomidine, which were sufficient for light but adequate sedation without hemodynamic compromise. The wide dose range for dexmedetomidine might have allowed the application of relatively higher doses in the trial by Eremenko and Chemova 32 , which might explain the longer MV duration due to potential deeper postoperative sedation.

The results of our study indicate that postoperative delirium develops twice as much with propofol sedation vs. dexmedetomidine. The group sedated with propofol had 25% postoperative delirium, compared to only 12% in the dexmedetomidine group, with a statistical difference slightly above the threshold ( p =0.059). This is consistent with the literature, as most of the studies have demonstrated a lower incidence of postoperative delirium in patients postoperatively sedated with dexmedetomidine compared to patients sedated with propofol and midazolam 33,34 .

A large meta-analysis by Wu et al 35 , including 1,387 cardiac surgery patients from 10 different trials, showed that the risk of delirium was lowered by 54% in patients receiving dexmedetomidine, which is consistent with our results. However, there are also large trials 4,36 whose results did not show a reduction in the incidence of postoperative delirium with dexmedetomidine sedation compared to other sedatives. We hypothesize that this could be attributed to hypotension and bradycardia, the most common side effects associated with dexmedetomidine.
Limitations

The primary limitation of our study is that additional medications that were prescribed during sedation were not analyzed, such as antipsychotics or opioids, which may have altered the patients' level of sedation and affected their time on MV and other outcomes.

The secondary limitation is the fact that all patients with a history of serious mental illness, delirium, and severe dementia were excluded from the study, as were patients with hepatic or renal dysfunction and heart failure with LVEF <40%. These patients represent the most vulnerable groups with increased risk for the development of postoperative delirium, hence the exclusion of such individuals might diminish the significance of dexmedetomidine for the prevention of postoperative delirium.

Future scopes should be focused on identifying patients with increased risk of prolonged MV and associated complications and implementing prevention measures in these individuals. Moreover, although the protocols for the prevention of postoperative delirium have been established, clinical trials investigating their use and results in routine clinical practice are still missing. Further investigations are required to validate the efficacy and safety of pharmacological prevention, as well as non-pharmacological measures, such as the open-door policy in the ICU, digital contact with family and friends, and other alternative methods.

Conclusions

Postoperative sedation with dexmedetomidine, compared to propofol, reduces the duration of MV but does not influence the length of stay in the ICU and length of hospitalization after open heart surgery. Postoperative delirium is less common in patients sedated with dexmedetomidine.
